en: Preface to the Ritual for the Longhua Repentance.

Composed by Ming Jinshi Zanzhii Yin, Grand Master of the Central Council (Zhongyi Dafu), formerly serving as Shangshu Lang of the Ministries of War and Justice in the Two Capitals, and currently retired from his post as Assistant Commissioner of the Censorate for Guangdong, Huguang, and other regions. Presented for Imperial Review.
By Imperial Decree, promoted to the rank of Fourth Class. Composed by Zhidao of Loujiang Army.

In the spring of the *Ren-shen* year of the Longqing era, while I was serving in the Ministry of Personnel (*Liubiao*), I obtained the *Dahui Pujue Chanshi Yulu* (The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dahui Puji).

Upon reading it, I could not help but strike my palm in approval. At that time, there was an elder named Zhang who spoke of the matters concerning the ten directions and the three periods of time. He asked: "Master Dahui [re-...]"
"Will you come again? I replied, "I have already come more than twice; I simply do not know how many *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* have passed.
He asked again, "When you come again, will there still be such sharp exchanges of wit (*jīfēng*)? I replied, "This coming time, I shall conceal the doctrine (*zōng*) and manifest practice (*xíng*).

Otherwise, I shall also employ the teachings (*jiào*) to clarify the doctrine. Twelve years later, in the *wàn lì* year of Jiǎshēn, I had already courageously retired from the turbulent stream and followed [the path].
At Jijian Hermitage on Tianchi Mountain, Qiansong De served as the Dharma Master for the lecture hall.

Knowing that his lineage traced back to the Dharma Master Wansong Lin, one day the conversation turned to Wansong’s origins, and [Qiansong] said, "Does Your Honor also know that my teacher was the reincarnation of Dahui?
Because I had previously harbored doubts and suspicions, I was startled and asked him about his life story and actual conduct.
Qiansong was one of the thousand who followed the Way; he may also be called a Dharma-son of [Zhili]. I alone wonder where Qiansong’s Dharma heir resides.
After Qiansong had passed away, there was a disciple of the Tiantai master Xiangxian Qing named Master Huanxing.
He was a unicorn among the Dharma gates. Having received his robe and bowl from Master Qing, he further sought instruction on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* from Qiansong.
Upon investigating the Way of Bodhidharma, his reputation spread far and wide. In the spring of the year Yiwu, we happened to meet at Yushan Temple in Wumen;
observing his conduct, which was unconventional and noble, and seeing that both his understanding and practice were transcendent, I regarded him as my equal, yet I harbored a secret doubt.

He said: "Are you not a true Dharma-son of the Thousand-Pine [Master]? It has been several years since we last parted. I have recently brought with me the various works from the *Fofa jintang bian* (The Compilation of the Buddhist Dharma as a Golden Wall) that I have edited, to verify our understanding against one another.

In the middle spring of the Dingwei year, I came to Wu and presented the twelve articles of the *Longhua chan yi* (Ritual for the Dragon Flower Repentance), which begins with the cultivation of correct faith and concludes with the contemplation of the single reality-mark (*ekasvabhāva-lakṣaṇa*). I request your instruction, for there are two [views] in the world..."
Ordinary people with these three great minds refuse to become men of liberation;
they would rather, amidst the five turbidities, attempt to steal the "arm-pit talisman" of the Old Śākyamuni, seeking directly to enter the gate of Maitreya at the Dragon Flower Assembly.
Elder, why begrudge me a few words as armor for my breast? I have long admired the Master’s realization and am further emboldened by this Bodhisattva of Great Resolve.
Upon opening this volume and reading it, I could not help but leap for joy.

The general gist is that because the world exclusively venerates the Pure Land and relies solely upon Amitābha, it fails to examine the vision of Maitreya, who dwells in Tuṣita to deliver sentient beings and swiftly enters the stage of non-retrogression.
This path is both swift and secure; yet, rather than proceeding from this place to roam the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), [people neglect it].
I, alone, rely on the nine grades to welcome you from afar; this is not what the Buddhas expect of a being of great resolve.
This thought is most earnest, and this vision is most correct. Yet, as for what is analyzed therein: which is exiting the triple world vertically?
Which is exiting the triple world horizontally? Which is exiting the triple world while remaining within it? And which is exiting the triple world by departing from it?
Regarding the three realms: which is neither identical to nor separate from them, yet transcends the three realms?

Within that transcendence of the three realms, furthermore, distinguish which constitutes the provisional teaching that simultaneously addresses the three vehicles, and which constitutes the real teaching that addresses the single vehicle alone.

Within the teaching of the single vehicle, further distinguish which is the gradual gate that reveals the real by opening up the provisional, and which is the [gate] that discards the provisional to return to the real.
The Round Gate (Enmyō). Thus, by way of the principal [teacher] and the capacity [of the audience], four distinct excellences are distinguished.
That it opens for sentient beings the true cause of the three assemblies at the Dragon Flower may be said to be both clear and urgent, leaving nothing omitted.

However, when I examine this through the *Lotus Sūtra*’s reality-limit (shinjitsu-sō), these twelve items—even for a master of illusions—belong to the provisional teaching (gonsetsu) and are not the ultimate teaching (jissetsu).
Who among people does not grow weary of gradual cultivation as being clumsy? Yet how can they know that the gradual is the cause for the sudden?

With the sole exception of the icchantika who has not yet turned their mind toward enlightenment, there is not a single person who does not enter the stage of Buddhahood through each and every moment (*kṣaṇa*).
Who among people does not rejoice in sudden awakening and sudden realization as being transcendent? Yet how can they know that the sudden is the step for the gradual? With the sole exception...
Before the first King of Majestic Sound (Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja), there was not a single person who did not attain the fruit of Buddhahood after three *asaṃkhyeya*-kalpas.

This internal message does not merely concern the threshold of "hearing in the morning and dying in the evening" as taught by the Sage of Confucius; rather, it concerns the realm beyond "knowing one's destiny" and "following the mind," which is difficult to express in words.
Since the Master of Illusions fears that those of middling and inferior capacity might believe in Sukhāvatī while doubting the Dragon Flower Assembly, he has provided this teaching.

Furthermore, fearing that those of the highest rank among the superior men might revere Longhua (Dragon Flower) while disparaging Sukhāvatī, I have employed much circumlocution and refined phrasing in my discourse.

This was intended to accommodate the capacities of both Confucians and Buddhists; thus, there are instances where my expressions were intentionally made flexible and versatile. We are disciples of the Master Kong;

the Master took the *Qian* hexagram’s "non-action" as the shore of the Way of upward-reaching transcendence, and the *Kun* hexagram’s "primordial creativity" as the foundation for downward-reaching immanence.

Regarding the true cause for study, one should not only practice the teachings of Amitābha, Maitreya, and others concurrently without contradiction, but should even unify them through a single principle.
What is there to rejoice in or loathe? Examining the current practice of Confucius, it was truly his desire to establish and lead sentient beings into the stage of non-retrogression;
is this not precisely the perfect cultivation of Mañjuśrī’s wisdom and Samantabhadra’s conduct combined?
As for this, does the learner indeed attain something within the gate of "learning below and reaching above"?
Although it may not be necessary to inquire further regarding the two Honored Ones, Amitābha and Maitreya, their Dharma is not a phenomenon external to our own mind.
Their Way, likewise, is not a Way external to the "One Thread" that the Master [Confucius] unified. If Amitābha truly has a karmic affinity with this land, then [his teaching] is exhaustive.
The pure lands within the realm of empty space are beyond counting; according to conditions and vows, what could not be possible?

If we discuss the way of the *I Ching*—ascending dragons and driving celestial chariots, or abiding in constancy and responding to the earth—it is precisely at this juncture between the passing of the Twin Trees and the future arrival of the Dragon Flower Assembly that the Confucian tradition stands firm, while Maitreya is perhaps gathering his followers.
The Buddha Śākyamuni and the Sage Confucius both sought to deliver those descendants who had not yet been saved;
that we today uphold the regulations of Confucius is precisely how we plant the causes for the Dragon Flower (Tuṣita) assembly.

Thus, our future worship of the Dragon Flower may well be the ultimate fulfillment of the will of Ni-fu (Confucius) that remained unfulfilled. My admiration for the Master of Illusions (the Buddha) is therefore no shallow matter. Hence...
I have composed this preface.
Written on an auspicious day in the second month of spring in the year of Dingwei during the Wanli era, at the Teyuezhai (愓若齋) in Wumen.
This concludes the first fascicle of the *Lianhua Xiuzheng Chan Yi* (The Ritual for Cultivating Realization through the Dragon Flower).
Written by the Śramaṇa Ruxing of Ciyun Temple on Mount Tiantai, who transmits the teachings:
In the world, there are those who, upon hearing of the World-Honored One Maitreya’s preaching of the Dharma at the Dragon Flower Assembly, immediately consign it to a high shelf.
To leave things to chance and hope for an encounter is like looking into a bag to find its contents; is this not lamentable?

This is because they do not know that those delivered at the three assemblies have predetermined limits from the outset. For instance, those delivered at the first assembly numbered nine hundred and sixty million people.
If two or three assemblies each reduce their numbers by two, how can we know that we shall not—by means of even a single practice or a single vow—be surely included among them?
To think otherwise is the height of delusion. If there are sentient beings of great resolve who wish for the future...
Dwelling in the city of Kukkuṭa-vyūha, he will travel daily upon the golden ground as level as the palm of a hand.

Enjoying a long life of eighty thousand years and partaking in the abundance of the four great treasuries, he shall encounter King Śaṅkha, proceed to the Dragon Flower Tree, behold Maitreya, become an Arhat,
realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and [serve] the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa in succession.
Those who receive this prediction should diligently cultivate these twelve expedient means.

At the end of their lives, they will certainly first be reborn in the Inner Court (Abhyantarika), where they shall behold the white tuft of hair between the Buddha’s brows and enter the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*). Thereafter, they will descend to birth alongside the Buddha to deliver those of a similar kind.
Are these not those who, by a single leap, enter directly into the stage of the Tathāgata? Now, based on various Mahāyāna sūtras and the *Dharmasthiti-sūtra*...

Colophon: Having composed this method of repentance to establish superior conditions for merit, I only pray that all who see, hear, or rejoice in it will strive to encourage its circulation, so that the teaching shall not be discarded because of the failings of individuals.
First, developing right faith; second, extensively seeking virtuous friends;
third, strictly upholding the precepts; fourth, generating the bodhicitta;
fifth, clearly delineating the ritual for establishing the maṇḍala; sixth, paying homage and inviting the Triple Gem.
Seventh, repentance for past transgressions; eighth, exclusive recitation of the Lotus Sutra;
ninth, the three jewels as the field of merit; tenth, general contemplation of Tuṣita;
eleventh, specific contemplation of the Dragon Flower [Buddha]; twelfth, mindfulness of the single true reality.
First, on the development of right faith:

Now, the eighty thousand Dharma-gates taught by the Tathāgata upon his appearance in the world were all intended to entice sentient beings to escape the burning house, mount the white ox-cart, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Since the teaching was first transmitted to the East, those with the capacity for the Mahāyāna have been as numerous as chessmen...
They spread the constellations of the stars and erected the Dharma-banner everywhere, transmitting the Buddha’s life-force of wisdom.

Now that the time since the Sage departed has grown ever more remote and the armies of Māra blaze fiercely, we rely upon the single gate of the Pure Land to circulate through this age of five turbidities. Herein, both the mind and the Buddha are manifest; it is a bridge and a ferry across the sea of suffering.
Since the teachings provide clear evidence, those who attain rebirth are not limited to one path: there are those taught to be born in the Buddha-land of Abhirati to behold the Tathāgata Akṣobhya.
Some are taught to be born in the Lapis Lazuli World and see the Buddha Bhaiṣajyarāja-prabha; some are taught to be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang) and see Amitābha and others.
These are those who depart from the three realms and transcend the three realms; they are called those who "transversely exit" the three realms.

There are teachings in which, through the five *sthāpacitta* (five stopping-minds) and so forth, one destroys the delusions of the four abodes (*catur-vāsana*) and is born in the Land of Common Residence (*sahā-loka-dhātu*), where one beholds the Buddha of the Tripiṭaka.

There are teachings in which one cultivates the sequential three contemplations (*tri-vipaśyanā*), destroys the twelve grades of ignorance (*avidyā*), realizes the twelve stages (such as the first stage through the tenth stage of the *Avataṃsaka*, as well as Equal Enlightenment and Sublime Enlightenment), and is born in the Land of True Reward (*bhūtārtha-pāripūri-kṣetra*), where one beholds the body of Vairocana. There are teachings in which one contemplates the three truths (*tri-satya*) in their totality, [realizing them] instantaneously...

Those who shatter the afflictions of the five stages, abide in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, are born in the Land of Tranquil Light, and behold the Dharmakāya of Vairocana—these have emerged from the triple world while remaining within it;
they are called those who "vertically transcend the triple world.

There are also those taught to be born in Tuṣita Heaven, where they behold Maitreya and hear the Dharma of non-retrogression; these do not immediately, nor do they depart from, transcend the triple world.

Alas! Since the categories [of teachings] are many and the capacities of beings are not uniform, and since there are differences between capacity and teaching, how could one establish the core intention without eloquence?
Now, regarding Maitreya in contrast to the Buddhas of other directions, there are briefly four points of distinction: first, concerning the principal; second, concerning the capacity.
Regarding the principal, there are again two parts: first, concerning a single Buddha; second, concerning all Buddhas.

Regarding the initial reference to "one Buddha": although the merits of all Buddhas—whether considered horizontally or vertically—were personally proclaimed by the golden mouth [of the Buddha], how could there be any difference in their excellence?

It is specifically for the sake of Amitābha that, because he has a karmic affinity with this land, great Bodhisattvas such as Nāgārjuna have either composed treatises to elucidate his virtues or have preceded others in practice to inspire people to believe and accept them. As the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "Beyond the west..."
Ten trillion lands away in the ten directions, there is a world named Sukhāvatī. In that land there is a Buddha named Amitābha.
Thus we know that this is the realm of Amitābha’s transformation, located ten trillion *kṣetras* from here;

yet by the power of the Buddha’s vows and the roots of goodness of sentient beings, one can reach it in the snap of a finger. In reality, when its extent is measured, it is ultimately far removed from this direction. Maitreya—

As the successor to the World-Honored One, Śākyamuni, he inherited the dharma-robes and the lineage of the thousand Buddhas from beneath the Bodhi tree at the Crane Grove (*Hulin*) until his parinirvāṇa.

Relying upon this Bodhisattva’s various skillful means, my dusty robes were cleansed; I was led to encounter the Dragon Flower (*Nāgapuṣpa*) assembly and was granted the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). Such is the power of his compassionate heart and vows.
He does not descend to Amitābha’s land; furthermore, he manifests as residing in Tuṣita, sharing the same desire realm as I. To raise one's head is to behold him;
he is the most proximate and the most intimate. This constitutes his foremost excellence.

Next, regarding the various Buddhas: if sentient beings aspire to be born in the Buddha-lands of other directions, the teaching masters of those regions will either dispatch transformation-Buddhas or transformation-bodhisattvas to emit light and welcome them.
If they seek birth in the Inner Court, then Maitreya Bodhisattva, surrounded by immeasurable devaputras, will personally go out to meet them. This is the second excellence.

Regarding the capacities of sentient beings, there are also two aspects. First, we shall distinguish between "separation" and "identity"; second, we shall distinguish the speed with which one perceives the Buddha. As for separation and identity:
if one wishes to seek rebirth in another land, one must necessarily leave this burning house and proceed to that cool, refreshing realm.

Even those of the highest capacity, though they know that birth is identical to non-birth, have not yet realized the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*) and thus are not without feelings of longing and aversion; how much more so for those of middling and lower capacities? Rebirth...
The "inner court" refers to these very three realms. Being unstained by the three realms, one does not perceive within them even the slightest phenomenon that can be grasped or rejected.
Therefore, without the exertion of longing for the pleasant or revulsion toward the unpleasant, one beholds the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā*). Thus, the Sūtra says:

"If there are sentient beings who do not loathe birth and death, but delight in being born in heaven, and who wish to become disciples of Maitreya, they must cultivate their minds and bodies with diligence..."
Furthermore, without seeking the severance of fetters and even without having yet generated the great vows, after the end of their life,
in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, they will immediately attain rebirth in Tuṣita Heaven, sitting cross-legged upon a lotus flower. This is the third excellence.
Next, to distinguish the speed with which one sees the Buddha: in the Western [Pure Land] there are nine grades of stages. Those of the superior grade see the Buddha immediately.
As for those of the middle and lower grades, it may take several days or even several kalpas before the flower blooms (as stated in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*:

those of the highest-superior grade see the Buddha upon birth; those of the high-middle grade see him when the flower blooms after one night; those of the high-lower grade see him when the flower blooms after one day and night; they see the Buddha after seven days. For those of the middle-superior grade, the flower blooms immediately, though it does not mention seeing the Buddha; for those of the middle-middle grade, the flower unfolds after seven days).

After half a kalpa, one becomes an arhat; this is the middle-low grade. After seven days of encountering Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, one passes through a small kalpa and becomes an arhat; this is the low-high grade. After seven days, the lotus blossoms; this is the low-middle grade. After six kalpas, the lotus blossoms; this is the low-low grade.
Only after twelve great kalpas have passed will the lotus flower open. Those born in the Inner Court sit upon the lotus and immediately behold Maitreya; thus the sutra says:
In future ages, when sentient beings hear of this Bodhisattva’s reputation for great compassion, they will pay homage and maintain mindfulness of him.
When such a person is about to die, the Bodhisattva will emit light from between his eyebrows and, together with various devaputras, rain down mandārava flowers to come and welcome them.
In an instant, that person will attain rebirth and encounter Maitreya, bowing their head in prostration before him without even raising it.
Recently, we were able to hear the Dharma and attain non-retrogression from the unsurpassed path; this is the fourth excellence.
All of this was due to the World-Honored One Śākyamuni’s bitter-mouthed exhortations, urging us to be born in Tuṣita.

If we had not followed his instructions—just as when a mother stands by one’s side with sincere and profound compassion, yet her child, out of folly, regards her as a stranger and willingly flees, refusing to stay—[we would not have attained this].
They drew near. Although the mother enticed him, the son departed swiftly for another place; such is the one who is truly to be pitied. From this day forward, among all practitioners:
there are those who have resolved their minds through the empowerment of the Buddha Śākyamuni’s compassion;

those who, having read the sutras on Maitreya’s ascent to Tuṣita, his descent to earth, and his attainment of Buddhahood, aspire to be born there; and those who recite the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Universal Worthy’s Exhortation*.

Chapter on Arousing the Resolve. Those who give rise to faith and joy in their hearts should practice with single-minded diligence. Relying upon this, they should cultivate with earnest application, practicing loyalty and filial piety with devotion;

with a compassionate heart, they shall not kill, but deliver all beings. I say that such a person, though dwelling in the sea of suffering, is fundamentally a vessel of the Mahāyāna whose roots do not regress.
In the past, within the teachings of immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, they have planted various roots of goodness.
Rooting oneself and giving rise to the unsurpassed vow, one gains entry into this gate. Because of entering this gate, one is called a Dharma Prince (*dharmaputra*).
Although dwelling amidst afflictions (*kleśa*), one is like the *utpala* flower; in a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), one roams through all samādhis.

These very four great elements are themselves the Medicine King (*bhaiṣajyarāja*), capable of curing all the ailments of the eight inversions. A single word uttered from the mouth becomes a banner of light, and that which is contemplated by the mind...

Alas! These are all great assemblages of the Dharma, inconceivable treasuries. Their giving and relinquishing are inexhaustible; they serve as the ship of Prajñā to ferry across those drowning in the sea of suffering.

Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are their supreme friends. With a single thought of awakening, they ascend to the stage of non-retrogression and directly transcend to the precious destination, rather than entering the illusory city.
At the Dragon Flower assembly, they shall be the leaders who proclaim the Way, making universal offerings throughout the lands of the ten directions.
Saha. They have accomplished the unsurpassed awakening of the Tathāgata, such that the praises of the Buddhas of the three periods of time can never exhaust it.
Some say that in the past, there were the three great Bodhisattvas—Maitreya (Tianqin), Asaṅga (Wuzhuo), and Siṃhabuddhi (Shizijue)—who led one another to seek rebirth in the Inner Court.
Master Shizijue resided in the outer courtyard his entire life and never beheld Maitreya.
When the Tiantai Master Zhiyi composed the *Ten Doubts*, he pointed out that [the path to] Tuṣita is difficult while [the path to] Sukhāvatī is easy;

those who insist it is difficult do not understand that human natures are not uniform and that karmic conditions vary from person to person. This is like Jia Shan, who abandoned doctrinal study for Chan and immediately ascended the patriarchal seat.
Xuanzang cast aside his innate nature and cultivated through practice until his fame surpassed that of all lands; Linji received three painful blows of the staff before awakening under Dayu;

Changqing broke seven cushions of rush matting before finally penetrating the truth upon rolling up the curtain. In each case, there was a specific condition to which they were linked; from the outset, there was no superiority or inferiority in their principles.
These medicines are all capable of curing disease—why must a skilled physician cling to a single prescription? This is why one attains rebirth in the Pure Land, or rebirth in the heavens above.
All follow their own inclinations. Whether reaching the distant or the near, they are all equalized by the compassionate light.
Although I now praise and extol this to inspire faith and acceptance, it is only appropriate to establish teachings according to the capacities of beings; the principle may well be so.

If one suspects that there is an outer court, or harbors doubts regarding the City of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), this is merely the practitioner’s own delusion—it is not due to any discrepancy in the Buddha’s power. This is especially true regarding the outer court and the city of doubt.
All are transformed by True Compassion and have been specifically placed here so that they may gradually behold the Buddha;

who then would dare to disparage Gautama on account of the three hundred million followers in Rājagṛha? Some say that those in the City of Doubt advance but do not retreat, and that those in the outer enclosure whose merit is exhausted will become wheel-turning kings.
This is because they do not know that this heaven has two diverging paths. There are sentient beings who, upon hearing the Mahāyāna teachings...

As for those who seek rebirth in the higher realms: because their faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) is not yet pure, the Bodhisattva’s compassionate mind causes them to dwell in the outer enclosure, awaiting their full maturation so that they may behold the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*).
This corresponds to the City of Doubt; all say they have not yet regressed.

Furthermore, there is a class of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), whether gods or humans, who have not heard the Great Dharma and exclusively cultivate the Lesser Vehicle or the non-Buddhist concentrations of the "unreached stage" (*anabhisamskāra-samādhi*); they merely hope for ascension.
To advance further without understanding non-arising (*anutpāda*) is like an unlearned bhikṣu whose merit is exhausted and who must continue to transmigrate.

If one claims that because the Pure Land (*Sukhāvatī*) has nine grades of stages, the three vehicles (*triyāna*) must all rely upon it, whereas Tuṣita teaches only the Dharma-gate of non-retrogression, then the position [of Tuṣita] would not be a grand progression;
would this not be too narrow? This is because one does not understand the subtlety of the mind and the transformative power of the land. The Buddha is fundamentally without birth. Nine...

Because the realms arise, the Buddha-realm also arises. Therefore, ordinary beings are born through the retribution of karma; the Buddhas are born through unconditioned compassion (*nirālamba-karuṇā*); and Bodhisattvas are born through the power of their vows.
Regarding birth through karmic retribution, it is not only the conditions of suffering in the three evil realms that are involved;

the three good realms are also conditions of suffering. Regarding birth through unconditioned [compassion], it is not only the four lands that constitute pure lands; the seven destinies [are also included].
All are pure lands. Puxian was a peppermint plant; the realm of animals is itself a pure land. Guanyin was Mianran;
the realm of hungry ghosts is itself a pure land. Devadatta entered the oil cauldron; hell is itself a pure land. Thus, Chan Master Guquan’s verse on his nirvana says:
"Today is the sixth day of the sixth month; Guquan has fully received his retribution. It is not that he ascends to heaven, nor is it..."

He entered hell and then stood transformed with his hands joined in *añjali*. If these beings were like the outspread wings of heaven, how could even the "gradual ascent" (*hongjian*) of a great bird restrain them?
There are nine ways of being born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*) through the power of vows, and likewise three ways in Tuṣita.

First, there is birth attained through both vows and practice—such as that of the Bodhisattva Maitreya (who possesses both the vow to seek birth there and the practice of benefiting sentient beings). Second, there is birth through practice alone, without a vow.
They attain birth [in the Pure Land], such as the Venerable Zhanran and other masters of Chan and the Teachings who did not seek rebirth in the Pure Land;
most were born in this heaven. There are also those who attain birth through aspiration alone without practice, such as the layman Bai Juyi.

Generally, within the Dharma of Śākyamuni, those who have refined a single precept, diligently practiced a single deed, or invoked the Name for even a single thought-moment, will eliminate births spanning hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.
Even those with the sin of death may attain birth in the Inner Court; otherwise, they shall likewise receive the prediction of the Way at the assembly of the Dragon Flower.

This is what is meant by "cutting off the flow at its source"—what narrowness could there be? As the ancients said: "If you wish to know the meaning of the Buddha-dharma, you must observe the conditions of time and circumstance."
Therefore, because the conditions for rebirth lie with Amitābha, Maitreya cannot but teach one to be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).

Because the conditions lie with Maitreya, Amitābha cannot but exhort one to encounter him at the Dragon Flower Assembly (Nāgapuṣpa). The lifespan of people today has become exceedingly short; the kalpa of weapons is near (the human lifespan will decrease until it reaches ten years, when the kalpa of weapons arises;

currently, the human lifespan is sixty years, and the kalpa of weapons is not far off). One must seek auspicious omens at Shicheng (during the winter of the Bingwu year of the Wanli era, in Shaoxing...).

At Mount Shicheng in Xinchang County, a five-colored *udumbara* flower grew from the foot of the stone Maitreya statue. As the hearts of both the clergy and the laity were harmonized—since people at the end of the Dharma all yearn for the Dragon Flower Assembly—will not the teaching of Tuṣita flourish?
A verse says: Maitreya is truly Maitreya, Manifesting hundreds of billions of transformation bodies.
From time to time he appears before the world, Yet the people of this age do not recognize him.
Some may say that being reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang) to encounter a Buddha of fruition is what is called supreme;

yet, since Maitreya resides as the "Successor" (Upapadya), his rank is at the final moment of mind of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi). Compared to Amitābha, he is still separated by one interval—how could he be superior?
This is because they do not understand the inconceivability of a Buddha’s wisdom. As the Sūtra says: "Only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully exhaust [this matter]. Therefore, Great Wisdom...

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to all Buddhas of the three periods of time within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

(Visualize that the past Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa and others, the present Buddha Śubhavyūharājasaṃkusumitābhijña and others, and the future Buddha Puṣparāja and others, all appear before me and accept my offerings.)

With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and invite all the Buddhas of the ten directions who eternally abide: (Visualize that the Buddhas of the ten directions, each endowed with the full marks and signs of perfection, emitting great radiance and surrounded by vast assemblies, come to this site of practice to accept my offerings.
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and invite the Mahāyāna Lotus Sūtra, the Sūtra on Rebirth in the Upper Realm, and the Sūtra on Attaining Buddhahood in the Lower Realm.
[Visualize] the profound and secret Dharma-treasures of the sūtras and so forth, all appearing before you, receiving my offerings.

With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat the Namah to all the eternally abiding Dharmas of the ten directions. [Visualize] the profound Dharma-treasuries taught by the Buddhas of the ten directions, all appearing at this site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), receiving my offerings.
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (visualize him riding upon a lion, surrounded by immeasurable bodhisattvas,
coming to this site of practice to accept my offerings). With single-minded devotion,
I take refuge in and entreat Samantabhadra Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (visualize him riding upon the white elephant king, surrounded by immeasurable bodhisattvas, coming to this [site of practice]).

At the site of enlightenment, they accepted my offerings during the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*. Because these bodhisattvas served as the presiding masters of repentance, they are listed at the end; whereas now, at the Dragon Flower [Assembly], Maitreya is the presiding master, and thus he should be placed at the beginning.

With a single mind, I reverently entreat: Namo Bhaisajyarāja Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, and Bhaisajyasamudgata Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. (In each case, direct the mind and perform the visualization as before.)
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas Avalokiteśvara and Akṣayamati.
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas Gadgadasvara and Śrīkūṭa.
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas Nityodyukta and Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāpratibhāna and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Jñānakośa.
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat the Bodhisattvas Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, Śūradatta, and Kṣitigarbha Mahāsattvas.

With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat the boundless asaṃkhyeya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, such as the Honored One Superior Conduct (Urdhvagama) from the lower direction; with single-minded devotion,
I take refuge in and entreat the Honored One Maitreya Bodhisattva, who currently resides in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace as the Regent.

[The Bodhisattva] Mahāsattva (visualizes this Bodhisattva as having a form like that of a celestial king, complete with the primary and secondary marks, emitting the radiance of great compassion, and surrounded before and behind by immeasurable sons and daughters of heaven, each holding various implements of offering).
Riding upon celestial palaces, they descend from the Tuṣita Heaven to the site of enlightenment to receive my offerings.
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat all the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of the non-retrogressive stages, such as Maitreya (Devaputra), who dwell in the Tuṣita Palace.

(Visualize that within the inner court of Tuṣita, Bodhisattvas of the non-retrogressive stages such as Devaputra and others—immeasurable and boundless—surround Maitreya and descend to the site of enlightenment to receive my offerings.)
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and invite the great *śrāvakas*, such as Upāli and Śāriputra,

as well as all the eternally abiding Saṃgha throughout the ten directions (*Imagine the assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and the sages of the ten directions gathering like clouds, arriving at this place of practice to receive my offerings*).
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and invite all the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings, both human and non-human, within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Together with their retinues,
they single-mindedly invited five billion devaputras from the Tuṣita Heaven, the deity Lohitākṣa, the five great deities,
and all the devaputras and devakanyās, each together with their respective retinues— thus invoking them one by one by name.
Recite this three times. When the invitation is concluded, the leader takes up the incense burner, stands together with the assembly, and makes this proclamation:
"I pray that our original teacher, Śākyamuni Bhagavān, Maitreya Sugata, and all the Buddhas, with your great kindness and great compassion, accept my invitation and come to this place of practice."
The Mahāyāna Lotus Sūtra, the Maitreya Bodhisattva’s Sūtra on His Rebirth Above, and the sūtras concerning his attainment of Buddhahood below—
may you take pity upon us, protect us, receive our precepts, and grant your invocation, coming now to this place of practice.
Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, Maitreya Bodhisattva, Upāli, Śāriputra, and all the assembly of holy ones— may you all, out of compassion,
accept my invitation and come to this place of practice. May all the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings,
the sons and daughters of the gods in Tuṣita Heaven, and the host of deities including the Lohitavāsas, all give rise to pity and accept my invitation.
I pray that you, this assembly of noble ones, will all bear witness.

I now wish, for the sake of all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions, to practice the unsurpassed Bodhi of the Mahāyāna and to destroy all heavy sins that obstruct the Path.
May I attain the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* and, in every thought-moment, extensively cultivate the field of merit of the Triple Gem. At the end of my life, may I be reborn above in Tuṣita Heaven.
Leading the inner court, they personally behold the light from the white tuft between the eyebrows—the mark of a great man—of Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Hearing the wondrous Wheel of Dharma, they realize non-retrogression. Within a single thought-moment, they universally deliver all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions.
Following Maitreya Bodhisattva, they descend to Jambudvīpa; when he attains perfect enlightenment beneath the Dragon Flower Bodhi tree, [they shall likewise do so].
We, together with King Śaṅkha and his various ministers and attendants, performed various offerings and exhorted him to turn the wheel of Dharma.
Having heard the teachings of the three assemblies, we became arhats, realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), and received the prediction of our future enlightenment.

Furthermore, we shall continue to make offerings to all the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, and throughout the limits of the future, we shall serve every World-Honored One without missing a single one. In this regard—
Before each Buddha, I shall extensively cultivate the myriad practices to benefit sentient beings and realize the ultimate path.
I reverently pray that Maitreya Bodhisattva and all the Triple Gem, by the power of their original vows, will accept my repentance and fulfill my aspirations, and so forth.

(Once the vow has been recited, one should again prostrate with the five limbs touching the ground. Rising, one should straighten the body and maintain a dignified demeanor, facing the Dharma seat. Burning incense and scattering flowers, one should personally proclaim verses of praise and offer various prayers of benediction.)
The Perfectly All-Knowing One, the Honored One among two-legged beings, is peerless in the world of gods and humans.
The World-Honored One of Ten Powers is most rare; he is the unsurpassed, most excellent field of merit.
Those who make offerings to him will be born in the heavens and, in the future, attain liberation and abide in nirvana.
I prostrate to the peerless one of great diligence; I prostrate to the compassionate Great Teacher.
(Having praised the Buddha with this verse, one should recite the aspiration:
By these roots of goodness from practicing the unsurpassed Mahāyāna and extolling the Buddha’s merits, I offer this merit to the devas and nāgas of the upper realms.

The eight classes of beings: the Great Brahma Heaven King, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, Yama and the five paths of rebirth, the six fast days, the eight kings, and the ghost-kings who spread diseases, each with their retinues;
the local deities of this land; and those within the monasteries who protect the True Dharma—on their behalf, as well as for those of the present...

To the Emperor, the Crown Prince, the Empresses and Consorts, the high ministers both internal and external, the common people throughout the realm, the monastics and their parents, virtuous and non-virtuous spiritual friends, the donors who build temples, and the faithful offerings from the ten directions—may these extend widely to all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm.
By virtue of these roots of goodness, may we cultivate with equanimity the two kinds of adornments: merit and wisdom, and together attain the state of non-arising, perfecting the seeds of Buddhahood.

The Path of Wisdom. (One should understand that body, speech, and mind pervade the Dharma-realm. One should praise the Triple Gem as being without birth or cessation, and devoid of intrinsic nature. Furthermore, with single-mindedness and upright physical deportment, one should successively pay homage to the Triple Gem previously invoked. Regarding the ritual of homage:

one should, in accordance with the Buddhas to whom one pays homage, contemplate with a sincere heart the Buddha’s Dharma-body, which is equal in measure to empty space and manifests forms according to objects, as if facing them before one's eyes, accepting my prostrations. One should know that my own body and mind are fundamentally empty and quiescent, lacking any characteristics of homage.

Because they are empty and quiescent, they can also manifest reflections before each and every Buddha throughout the Dharma-realm, such that my body is present before all. Thus, one should prostrate with one’s head to the ground before all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas; in every case, it is thus.)

Visualize. Again burn incense, recite the names [of the Buddhas], and prostrate. The Three Jewels to whom one pays homage during the six periods of day and night are all as listed below, without exception).

With single-minded reverence, pay homage to the Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha. (The visualization says: "The nature of the one who prostrates and the object of prostration is empty and quiescent; the mutual resonance of cause and response is inconceivable.

This place of my practice is like a celestial jewel, within which the Tathāgata Śākyamuni appears as a reflection. My own body and shadow appear before Śākyamuni; with head touching his feet, I take refuge and pay homage. For the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas listed below, each should be modified according to their respective name, saying: "[Name]...")
Within the manifested shadows of the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, may my own shadow appear before such-and-such a Buddha, and so forth.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the past Buddha Prabhūtaratna;
with single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Śākyamuni Buddhas of the ten directions who have manifested as emanations.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Honored Buddha Maitreya of the future;
with single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the ten Buddhas of the ten directions, such as the Buddha Bhadraśrī of the East;
with single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Buddhas Candrasūryapradīpa and Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū of the past from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
With a single mind, I pay homage to all the Buddhas of the past:
the thousand Buddhas of the Adorned Eon (*Vibhūṣita-kalpa*), the seven World-Honored Ones, and all the Buddhas of the past throughout the ten directions.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to all the Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions as mentioned in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*,
such as the Buddha Prabhūtaratna (宿王華智), the Buddha Ratnatejobhyudgatarāja (寶威德上王),

and others; with single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Buddhas of the eight directions as mentioned in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, such as the Buddha Akṣobhya (阿閦) and the Buddha Meruśikhara (須彌頂).
I single-mindedly pay homage to the sixteen princes who are currently present as Buddhas;
I single-mindedly pay homage to all the Buddhas of the present Bhadrakalpa throughout the ten directions;
I single-mindedly pay homage to the future Buddha Padmaprabha within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*; and I pay homage to the Buddha endowed with thousands of millions of radiant marks.
I pay single-minded homage to all Buddhas of the future;
I pay single-minded homage to the thousand Buddhas of the Constellation Eon throughout the ten directions; I pay single-minded homage to all Buddhas of the future throughout the ten directions;
and I pay homage to the Honored Images and Relics, the Stūpas and Wondrous Pagodas, and to the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
With my whole body as a precious stūpa,
I single-mindedly pay reverent homage to the Mahāyāna Sutra of the Lotus Blossom of the Fine Dharma, the Sutra on Maitreya Bodhisattva’s Ascent to Tuṣita Heaven,
the Sutra on Maitreya’s Descent to Be Reborn, the Sutra on His Attaining Buddhahood, and all the honored sutras of the ten directions. Ten.
With single-minded devotion, I pay respectful homage to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the true and pure Dharma Jewel of the two divisions;
with single-minded devotion, I pay respectful homage to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata;
with single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas Avalokiteśvara and Akṣayamati;
with single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas Gadgadasvara and Śrīkūṭa.
With single-minded reverence, I pay homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas Nityodyukta and Mahāsthāmaprāpta;
with single-minded reverence, I pay homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas Mahāpratibhāna and Jñānakośa;
with single-minded reverence, I pay homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña and Dharaṇīdhara.
With single-minded reverence, I pay homage to the boundless asaṃkhyeya bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the lower direction, such as Śūraṅgama and others;
with single-minded reverence, I pay homage to all the great śrāvakas, including Upāli, Śāriputra, Ānanda, and the rest;
with single-minded reverence, I pay homage to the great bodhisattvas of skillful means in the ten directions, as well as the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the noble sages who have attained the Way.
The Sangha, with one mind, pays reverent homage to Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, who currently resides in the Tuṣita Heaven palace.

(One should perform three prostrations. Since this Bodhisattva is the presiding master of the Dragon Flower Assembly, the practitioner should, with a sincere heart, kneel on the right knee before this Bodhisattva, confess all transgressions, and make great vows. As for the other Buddhas and Bodhisattvas:)
May they all bear witness. Universally radiating rays of compassionate light, may they bestow their protection upon the practitioner so that all aspirations are fulfilled.
(7) Seventh, the Practice of Repenting Past Offenses:

Once the practitioner has finished prostrating to the Buddha, they should maintain upright posture and dignified demeanor, burn incense, scatter flowers, and visualize the Triple Gem filling the space.
The void, Maitreya Bodhisattva, and immeasurable sons of heaven, surrounded by their retinues, are ever present before me.
For this reason, I shall now perform the rite of repentance for the sake of all sentient beings. Why is this?

It is because I and all sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm have been deluded since beginningless time, following after the six sense organs and committing the ten evil deeds, thereby sinking into the realms of suffering and undergoing [their retribution].

Recompenses are manifold; the long night is dark and obscure, where few emerge only to sink back again. How can one not find this tragic? Yet, although the nature of sin is empty, its retribution is never lost.

If one is able to repent of one's sins by realizing that they are immediately empty—like a flake of snow falling upon a red furnace—and cultivate the true according to illusion—like a square pearl facing the bright sun—then the Buddhas of the ten directions extol the power of such repentance.

One who is called a "valiant warrior" (kṣatriya) is capable of accomplishing any task. Now, before the Triple Gem, raining tears and weeping with grief, I shall declare the transgressions of the six sense faculties.

Speaking aloud myself, I say: "For the sake of the four debts of gratitude, the three realms of existence, and all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm, I vow to sever the three obstructions and take refuge in repentance.
(Having prostrated once and knelt again, silently cultivate the ten minds of contrition and compliance, and then perform the repentance, saying: I, Bhikṣu [Name], [state your name].
And for all sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm, I repent with a sincere heart:

from time immemorial, I and all sentient beings have been shrouded by ignorance, deluded and inverted, and through the unwholesome actions of the six sense organs and the three karmas, we have extensively committed manifold transgressions.
The eye covets various forms. Because it is attached to forms, it craves the sensory objects (*viṣaya*). Because it craves these objects, it receives a female body.
In every birthplace throughout successive lives, it is deludedly attached to various forms. Forms ruin my eyes; as a slave to affection and craving, forms thus cause me to act.
Wandering through the three realms, one is driven by these debased afflictions; blind and seeing nothing, the ears pursue external sounds, creating all manner of transgressions.
When hearing sublime sounds, the mind gives rise to delusion and attachment; when hearing harsh sounds, it stirs up the hundred and eight kinds of afflictions that act as thieves and harmer.
Such is the evil ear; it reaps evil consequences, constantly hearing evil sounds because of its perverted hearing.

Consequently, one shall fall into the evil realms, reaching remote lands with false views where the True Dharma is not heard. One is deluded and attached everywhere, without a moment’s pause. The nose greedily craves fragrant scents.
If men or women encounter various delicacies and diverse fragrances, they become deluded and confused;
their fetters and latent tendencies are stirred, and the thieves of affliction all rise from their slumber. Immeasurable karmic offenses increase because of this craving for fragrance.

Through the discrimination of various consciousnesses caused by this greed for scent, they become stained and attached everywhere, falling into the cycle of birth and death to undergo various bitter retributions. Their tongues crave various flavors, thereby harming the multitude...
Born [into such states], they violate all the precepts and open the gates to negligence. They engage in false speech, frivolous talk, harsh words, and double-tongued speech;

they slander the Triple Gem and praise and propagate wrong views. They utter useless words, incite strife and discord, and declare what is not the Dharma to be the Dharma, and what is the Dharma to be not the Dharma.

These thorns of various evil karmas, which sever the Wheel of the True Dharma, arise from the faculty of the tongue; within what is not meaningful, they employ many stratagems with forceful persistence.

It is said that such offenses are immeasurable and boundless. Clad in various tactile sensations, one commits manifold transgressions—namely, regarding the male and female bodies, their softness, smoothness, and all such tactile contacts—one is deluded and lacks understanding;
with afflictions blazing intensely, one gives rise to the three unwholesome actions:
killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. Thus, one creates great enmity and bondage for all sentient beings, committing acts of rebellion and violating the precepts. And so forth...

They go so far as to burn down stupas and monasteries and consume the property of the Triple Gem without any sense of shame. Their minds are greedily attached to various phenomena; deluded and ignorant, they fail to understand.

Following after their objects of perception, they give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion. Such perverse thoughts can produce the ten non-virtuous actions and the five heinous crimes of immediate retribution.
They are like monkeys and like sticky glue; they cling greedily everywhere, pervading all six sensory faculties. Just as...
These evil karmas of the six sense organs pervade the twenty-five states of existence within the three realms.

In every place of birth, they can further increase ignorance, old age, and death, as well as the twelve links of suffering. There is no hardship among the eight heterodoxies and eight difficulties that one does not undergo.

The retributions of such evil karma are immeasurable and boundless; they cannot be fully described. Although the Buddhas of the ten directions constantly abide in the world, their Dharma-sound does not...

Exquisite fragrance fills all quarters; the flavor of the Dharma abounds throughout space. Pure radiance is emitted, illuminating and touching all things. The eternally abiding wondrous principle pervades the void.
Since beginningless time, my six sense-faculties have been internally blind and my three karmas have been shrouded in darkness.

Thus, I have neither seen, nor heard, nor awakened to, nor known [this truth]. Due to these causes and conditions, I have long been submerged in birth and death, traversing hundreds of thousands of millions of evil realms.
Kalpas will pass, yet there will never be a time of emergence. As the Sūtra says: "Śākyamuni is named Vairocana, pervading all places.
One should know that all dharmas are entirely the Buddha-dharma. Through false conceptualization and discrimination, one undergoes various torments;
this is to perceive impurity within Bodhi and to give rise to fetters within liberation. Only now does one begin to awaken."
I give rise to profound shame and remorse; I give rise to great fear. I recite and uphold the Great Vehicle, the exceedingly deep ocean-treasury.
I take refuge in Maitreya Bodhisattva and all the World-Honored Ones. I burn incense and scatter flowers, confessing and repenting my transgressions without daring to conceal them.
By these causes and conditions, may all the various evils arising from the six sense organs and three karmas of myself and all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm [be extinguished].
Those already arisen, those presently arising, and those that will arise in the future; whether committed by oneself, incited in others, seen, heard, or rejoiced in;

whether remembered or not, suspected or not, concealed or revealed—may they all be ultimately pure. (Having finished the repentance, take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem. At each of the six periods of day and night, recite this three times.)

If time is short, a single recitation may suffice. Next, perform the rite of exhortation: "I, the bhikṣu [Name], together with all sentient beings of the dharma-realm, sincerely exhort [the Buddhas]."

The infinite Buddhas of the ten directions and the Dharma-realm, we pray that you remain long and turn the wheel of Dharma. May all sentient beings endowed with consciousness return to their original purity;

thereafter, may the Tathāgatas enter eternal abiding. When the Holy Honored One Maitreya attains perfect enlightenment, may I, along with the king, ministers, and the great assembly, exhort him to turn the unsurpassed, subtle, and wondrous wheel, so that he may grant us predictions of enlightenment at his three assemblies. (Having made this request, take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem.)

Whether three times or once, as you wish. Next is the rite of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), which is performed as follows: "I, the bhikṣu [Name], with a sincere heart, rejoice in the various merits of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
in the wholesome deeds of ordinary beings, whether in stillness or agitation, characterized by form; and in all karma, both with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*)."
I now rejoice in each and every one [of these deeds]. (Having rejoiced, take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem. Next, perform the rite of dedication as follows:

Bhikṣu [Name], together with all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, with a sincere heart dedicates all the merit cultivated through the three karmas to making offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Until the end of the future, for all beings throughout space, may they rely upon this merit to seek the Buddha-way. (Having performed the dedication, take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem. Next, proceed...)

The Method for Making Vows: The practitioner should reflect: "From beginningless time until now, although I and all sentient beings have diligently practiced various virtues and meditative concentrations, because we did not make vows, these merits had nowhere to be directed and we failed to attain supreme and wondrous liberation.

Therefore, all the merits of the Buddhas of the ten directions and the great Bodhisattvas are established entirely by relying upon the King of Vows of Samantabhadra. For this reason, as I now cultivate various samādhis and perform the practice of repentance, I likewise rely upon Samantabhadra to make great aspirational vows.
Then, kneeling single-mindedly with one knee on the ground, burning incense and scattering flowers, one should chant:
Bhikṣu [Name], for the sake of all sentient beings throughout the entire dharma realm, has made this vast and sublime vow:

"Although we have been born in the age of the final dharma, we have encountered a holy era in which the Three Jewels flourish; we have heard the Mahāyāna teachings and know that there is the Bodhisattva Maitreya."

Having received the prediction of one birth, he currently resides in Tuṣita Heaven and shall, in the future, fill the position of the successor in this world, attaining unsurpassed enlightenment beneath the Dragon Flower Bodhi tree.

There, in three assemblies, he will deliver sentient beings. For these reasons, one should give rise to faith and joy, resolve upon the bodhicitta, not abandon the Sahā world, and not seek the mere severing of fetters;
rather, relying on the wisdom of the emptiness of nature, one should cultivate all roots of goodness and study...

Recite the profound Dharma-treasury of the Mahāyāna; uphold the prohibitive precepts without deficiency in dignified deportment. Regarding the Three Jewels as fields of merit, cultivate them exactly according to the teachings.
Recite the great name of Maitreya’s great compassion, burn various famous incenses, and make offerings of exquisite flowers.
Throughout the six periods of day and night, practice the profound samādhi. Dedicate these merits to all sentient beings, vowing that they may first be born in Tuṣita.
I lead my inner court and shall next encounter the Dragon Flower Assembly. I pray that Maitreya Bhagavān, Śākyamuni Buddha, and all the Triple Gem will appear as my witnesses.
May their compassionate power protect me and their light of mercy shine upon me, so that my repentance may be purified and my aspirations fulfilled.
At the time of my death, may I be free from all illness and suffering, and with right mindfulness present before me, enter as if into meditative absorption.
I personally beheld Maitreya Bodhisattva, who manifested the marks of a Great Being and emitted light from the tuft of white hair between his brows.
Together with various devaputras, he performed celestial music and, holding many heavenly flowers, came to welcome me.

In the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, I immediately attained rebirth in the Tuṣita Heaven upon a lotus flower, sitting there in the full lotus posture. I heard the devaputras uttering words of praise:

"Excellent! Let me take refuge in the Lord of Devas, Maitreya. At that time, by gazing intently at the white tuft of hair between his brows, I shall immediately transcend the heavy sins of birth and death spanning hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas.

May the Bodhisattva preach the unsurpassed, wondrous Dharma for me, so that I may become firm and never retreat from the mind set on the path to Bodhi, suddenly entering hundreds of thousands of samādhis, and thereafter follow him."

When the Bodhisattva descends to Jambudvīpa in the city of Ketumatī, he will manifest as a noble kinsman, or as a prince, a minister, an official, a commoner, a householder, or one of the six teachers of pure conduct. Through various skillful means, he will transform those of his own kind.

When Maitreya attains the Way, we shall follow King Śaṅkha to first entreat him to turn the wheel of the sublime Dharma. At the first assembly under the Dragon-Flower tree, we shall hear the subtle [Dharma].
Through this sublime Dharma, they awaken to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) and receive the prediction of enlightenment (*bodhi-vyākaraṇa*).

They shall also serve and make offerings to all the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, and throughout the Nakṣatra Kalpa, they shall extend their reach to the ten directions to all future Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, who are yet to appear in the world.
I shall make offerings to them all and receive their prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).

Furthermore, from this day forward until the end of the future, may I fulfill great vows and practices, possessing supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and eloquence (*pratibhāna*), manifesting bodies throughout the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), preaching the Dharma according to the capacities of beings, and delivering all infinite sentient beings, causing them to attain the Buddha-way without end.
Until the realm of empty space is exhausted and the realm of sentient beings is exhausted, and until karma and...
While afflictions or latent tendencies may come to an end, this King of Vows of mine shall never come to an end.

Having made this vow, take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem (reciting it once if time is short, three times if there is ample time; let the frequency follow one’s inclination). Upon finishing the recitation, perform three prostrations. Once the practitioner has made this vow, they shall give rise to great joy.

They will be reborn in the Inner Court and will certainly behold Maitreya at his Dragon-Flower Assembly, receiving the prediction of Bodhi. In every thought-moment, may this King of Vows constantly manifest before them, like my compassionate mother who never leaves my side. May all wholesome dharmas be cultivated in reliance upon it. At the moment of death, as for all karmic [obstacles]...

All [obstacles] have been dispersed. Only this King of Vows acts as a great guide, leading me upward to be born in the higher realms, so that I may hear the Dharma of non-retrogression and reach the ultimate ocean of fruition; it is through reliance on this that I achieve my goal. Because I have made this vow, it is like crossing over existence by means of a boat, or like a cripple obtaining a staff.

Though various metaphors and explanations were used, they could never be exhausted. Within the prison of the triple world, I have attained great fearlessness; the murderous ghost of impermanence does not dare to look upon me directly. Through the interconnection of the vital energies (*nāḍī*) with Samantabhadra, I act as a Great King of Physicians amidst the paths of sentient beings.

Having entered the stream of the Dharma, you should rejoice within yourself. Once you have made your vow, you should further, in a single thought-moment, rectify your physical demeanor and circumambulate the Dharma seat to the right, burning incense and scattering flowers, walking with calm and measured steps while mentally recollecting the Triple Gem, filling the entire site of enlightenment.
All possess my own body; circumambulating them in worship, I recite:
Homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions! Homage to the Dharma of the ten directions! Homage to the Sangha of the ten directions!
Homage to Śākyamuni Buddha! Homage to Prabhūtaratna Buddha!
Homage to the Buddha Śākyamuni, the Emanation Buddhas; homage to the future Buddha Maitreya;
homage to the Lotus Sūtra; homage to the Sūtra on Attaining Buddhahood in This Very Life;
homage to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī; homage to the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.

Homage to Maitreya Bodhisattva (recite this three times). Having finished, return to your original position. With a composed mind and dignified deportment, burn various sublime incenses and recite the *Buddhabhāṣita-maitreya-bodhisattva-ūrdhva-janma-tuṣita-svarga-sūtra*, or the "Chapter on the Practice of Peace and Bliss," or the "Chapter on the Universal Virtuous One’s Exhortation.

You should recite these aloud and clearly, neither too slowly nor too hurriedly, with every syllable distinct. Furthermore, you must realize that these sounds, as well as the body and mind, are like echoes, like illusions, like clouds, and like shadows.

Moreover, you should perceive that sound is entirely identical to the Dharma-nature; because the Dharma-nature is all-pervasive, my voice likewise pervades the ten directions and the entire Dharma-realm. Through this, I make offerings to the Triple Gem and extend [the merit] to all sentient beings, causing them all to attain awakening and resolve to attain Bodhi.

With a focused mind, when you have finished reciting the sutra, again burn incense and circumambulate to the right while chanting: "Namo Maitreya Bodhisattva," either one hundred times or one thousand times, as many times as you wish. Next, perform the Three Refuges according to the Dharma; you should maintain single-minded, correct mindfulness.
(Recite these words aloud:
"I take refuge in the Buddha; may all sentient beings realize the Great Way and give rise to the unsurpassed mind.
I take refuge in the Dharma; may all sentient beings enter deeply into the treasury of the scriptures, their wisdom as vast as the ocean."
Taking refuge in the Sangha, one should wish that all beings preside over great assemblies without any hindrance, and pay homage to the noble multitude.

(Having completed the Three Refuges, this concludes one session of Buddha-activity among the six periods. The practitioner should then proceed to the place for seated meditation. At their convenience, they should adjust their breath for a short while, then put on clean robes and the *saṃghāṭī*, and recite the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Ritual of the Lotus Samādhi*.

All six periods of practice should be performed within the *dharmadhātu* (meditation hall). If there are no more than ten people, it is acceptable as the number is small; now, however, the number has increased to twenty-five. Even if the meditation hall is spacious, one must still...)

A separate place for reciting scriptures is established. Previously, while within the *daochang*, one had stood to recite the *Sūtra on Rebirth in the Upper Realms*; now, outside the *daochang*, one sits to read the *Lotus Sūtra*. Previously, one might have recited only the "Peaceful Practices" chapter or the "Exhortation of Samantabhadra" chapter;

now, one reads one fascicle, two fascicles, or the entire work—thus there are these differences. However, the place for reciting scriptures must not be too far from the *daochang*, but must be kept very close. When the practitioner recites with the sound of a *bai* chant, both should maintain the same visualization and offerings to the Triple Gem as before.

Regarding the ritual of *samādhi*, one must first have thoroughly mastered one complete copy of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Since the practitioners here are numerous, their capacities—whether sharp or dull—are difficult to equalize; thus, it may not be necessary to complete the full recitation, provided one is simply proficient and well-versed in the entire text.

The commentary: This is to ensure that the phrasing and punctuation are clear and not confused. However, regarding the method of recitation, one must not rely solely on the murmuring of the lips; one should instead silently comprehend the meaning and intent. After a long time, one will naturally attain entry into the *svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī*.

Furthermore, during the six periods of the day, one should recite the *Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra* during the three daytime periods. During the three nighttime periods, one should recite only the *Sukhāvatī-vyūha-sūtra* or the *Anraku-gyō-hon* (Chapter on the Easy Practice), at which point [other recitations] should cease. One must sit exclusively in meditation so that contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) is perfected, leading to entry into the inconceivable realm.

○ Regarding the eighth point, the exclusive recitation of the Lotus Sūtra, there are three reasons for requiring such exclusive recitation. First, the Dragon Flower [Buddha] is like the ocean; though the paths differ, they all lead to the same destination.
Why then choose one over another? It is only feared that the practitioner’s aspirations may not be unified and their direction unsettled, whereby scattered good deeds will daily dissipate.

Then the mind of refined unity will be dissipated. Furthermore, if one restrains the mind to a single object—like an archer aiming at a target—the skill will become unified and the essence of the Way will easily manifest.
Second, the *Lotus Sūtra* itself calls itself the "King of Sūtras"; who could surpass it?
Third, this sūtra begins with Maitreya expressing doubt and concludes with Samantabhadra exhorting practice; the scripture states that if there is anyone who upholds it...

If one reads and recites [this] and understands its meaning and intent, at the end of that person’s life, a thousand Buddhas will extend their hands to them, causing them to be free from fear and not fall into the evil realms.
They shall immediately go to the Tuṣita Heaven to the place of Maitreya Bodhisattva.

Maitreya Bodhisattva possesses the thirty-two marks of a great man and is surrounded by a multitude of great bodhisattvas, as well as hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of celestial maidens as his retinue.

By being born therein, there are such merits and benefits as these. Therefore, the wise person should single-mindedly write it themselves, or cause others to write it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, maintain right mindfulness of it, and practice according to its teaching.

Because of this principle, one should cause them to recite it with devotion. Furthermore, those who merely uphold the sutra consist of three types of persons, which must also be distinguished: first, those for whom the words and meaning...
To be fully endowed [with both] is the superior grade, such as those like Aśvaghoṣa, Nāgārjuna, and other Mahāyāna masters, as well as Tiantai Zhiyi and others.
Second, to have the mind penetrate the meaning while not being familiar with the text is the middling grade, such as those like Caoxi the Sixth Patriarch and others.
Third, to be skilled only in the text while remaining ignorant of the meaning is the inferior grade, such as Fada.
"Venerable Master," it is so. Furthermore, there are two kinds of recitation: first, complete recitation; second, incomplete recitation.

Complete recitation refers to reciting the entire work. Incomplete recitation is also called partial recitation; for example, single-mindedly upholding only the "Chapter on Peaceful Conduct" (*Anle-xing pin*) according to the teaching.
There are also practitioners who lack the disposition for recitation, such as those who would rather recite [the name of] a broom.

O Kāśyapa, if one now wishes to see Maitreya, it is sufficient to firmly uphold even a single four-line verse, which is also called "reciting a portion. If we rely on what is said in the "Dharma Master" chapter—
that for those who hear even a single verse, a single phrase, or even a single thought of sympathetic joy regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*,
I shall bestow upon them all the prediction that they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi— it is clear that the merit of the whole is equal to that of the immeasurable.
The Ritual for Cultivation and Realization upon Encountering the Dragon Flower [Buddha], Scroll Two.
The Ritual for Cultivation and Realization upon Encountering the Dragon Flower, Scroll Three.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Ruxing, a Dharma-transmitting contemplative of Ciyun Temple on Mount Tiantai.
○ Regarding the ninth section, "The Supreme Teaching on the Field of Merit of the Three Jewels":
previously, one was instructed specifically to recite the *Lotus Sūtra* based on the "Exhortation of Samantabhadra" chapter.

Now, one is directed to extensively cultivate the field of merit of the Three Jewels based on the *Dharmāloka-vyūha-sūtra*. Since these two explanations differ, it is necessary to open two gates; this is what is meant by "converging like spokes."

They proceed in tandem, adorning the primordially existent *dharmakāya*. Furthermore, the *Maitreya’s Ascent to Tuṣita* Sūtra and other scriptures all contain the meaning of extensively cultivating [virtuous practices].
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "By means of the causes and conditions of merit and virtue, one attains birth in that land.

If one seeks rebirth in Tuṣita or at the Dragon Flower Assembly (*Nāgapuṣpa*), how could it be possible without cultivating the myriad practices? The *Dharmasthitistava* says: "If kings, ministers, elders..."
Laymen and laywomen, all such donors, within the true Dharma of the present Śākyamuni Buddha, are able to perform the work of a Buddha;
they plant roots of goodness for themselves or instruct others to plant them, namely by means of the seven treasures: gold, silver, pearls, jade, and precious stones.
Whether using incense materials, brass, copper, iron, wood, stone, or clay;
or by means of silk threads or painted colors, they fashion images of the Buddha and stūpas, whether large or small, even as small as the size of a finger joint;
or they offer worship with incense, flowers, and various exquisite offerings, whether many or few—by such roots of goodness as these, they [attain merit].
By the power of this, when Maitreya Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, they will obtain a human body with great excellence.

Within that Buddha’s first assembly, through pure faith, they will renounce worldly life and leave the household. Having shaved off their hair and beard and donned the dharma robes, they will join the noble community.
Thereupon, by the power of their former vows, they will immediately attain nirvāṇa. This is called the first planting of roots of goodness for the sake of the Buddha’s work.

As for the "roots": it refers to the karmic fruits obtained by kings, ministers, commoners, and all patrons who, within the current True Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha, are able to perform acts of Dharma, planting roots of goodness themselves or instructing others to do so.
That is to say, regarding all Mahāyāna sūtras within the Mahāyāna Sūtra Piṭaka that correspond to the profound emptiness (śūnyatā),
and so forth, even down to a single four-line verse, whether one recites them oneself, teaches others to recite them, or reads them oneself.

Whether causing others to read it, or upholding it oneself, or causing others to uphold it, or explaining it oneself, or causing others to explain it; or by respectfully making offerings to the Dharma Master,
or respectfully making offerings to the scriptural scrolls, and so forth— by the power of such roots of goodness as these,
when Maitreya Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, one will successfully obtain a human body and, in that [realm]...
In the second assembly, those who, with pure faith, renounce the ways of the household life to go forth into homelessness,
shave off their hair and beards, don the dharma robes, and having joined the noble assembly, attain nirvāṇa through the power of their former vows—
this is called the second kind of fruit and retribution obtained by those who plant roots of goodness for the sake of the Dharma. This applies to kings, ministers, commoners, and others as well.
All these donors, within the true Dharma of the present Śākyamuni Buddha, are able to perform services for the Saṃgha and plant roots of merit for themselves,
or teach others to do so— namely, the community of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs. Whether by regular invitation or according to circumstances,
on the first day of the month, or the eighth day, or the fifteenth day, they provide offerings of vegetarian feasts, or go [to the monastery].

Within a monastery, whether making offerings to a single individual or to the assembly, or serving as an attendant; or making offerings to those practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), or making offerings to those who preach the Dharma;

or seeing someone wishing to study and propagate the True Dharma, listening to it from a teacher, one does not create obstacles for them, but provides what they need for their well-being so that they do not become timid or retreat. Or, having established...
For five years, they held an unrestricted almsgiving assembly (*pañcavārṣika*), or gave to the Saṃgha of the four directions,
providing monasteries, as well as seats and bedding, or offering bells, gongs, gardens, groves, and similar items to make offerings to the community of monks. By the power of such roots of virtue,
when Maitreya Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, they will obtain a human body and, within that Buddha’s third assembly, through their purity...
With faith, they renounce the ways of the household life and go forth into homelessness. Having shaved off their hair and beards and donned the dharma robes, they join the noble assembly.
By the power of their prior vows, they immediately attain *nirvāṇa*. This is called the third fruit obtained by those who plant roots of goodness for the sake of the Saṃgha.
