Furthermore, the *Maitreya-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* states: "At that time, Maitreya Buddha, seeing all..."
The great assembly thought to themselves: "These people have not come to me for the sake of the pleasures of rebirth in heaven, nor for the sake of the pleasures of this present life;
rather, they have come solely for the sake of the causes and conditions for the eternal bliss of Nirvana. These people...
All of them have planted various roots of goodness within the Buddha-dharma. Śākyamuni has sent them to entrust them to me;
therefore, they have now all come to my presence, and I now receive them.
These people have either come to my presence having cultivated various merits by reciting, reading, analyzing, and determining the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma Piṭakas; or else—
Those who give clothing and food to others, maintain the precepts, and possess wisdom—having cultivated these merits, they come to my presence.
Or those who offer banners, canopies, flowers, and incense to the Buddha—having cultivated these merits, they come to my presence. Or those who practice giving and observe the fasts.

Cultivate a mind of loving-kindness. Practice these meritorious deeds and come to me; or, for the sake of suffering sentient beings, cultivate this merit so that they may obtain happiness and come to me;
or, through the practice of precepts and patience, cultivate pure loving-kindness and come to me with such merit;
or, by providing the Sangha with constant food, holding fast-day assemblies, and establishing dharma-meetings, make offerings [and come to me].

They partake of food and cultivate these meritorious deeds, coming to my presence; or by means of upholding the precepts, extensive learning, the cultivation of meditative concentration, and untainted wisdom, they come to my presence through these merits; or there are those who erect stupas and make offerings to the relics.
"By this merit, you have come to my presence. Excellent, Śākyamuni Buddha!
You are able to skillfully teach and transform hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings such as these, causing them to come to my presence.
After Maitreya Buddha had thus praised Śākyamuni Buddha three times, he then preached the Dharma, saying: "You sentient beings have been able to perform what is difficult."
In that evil age, among people who are greedy, lustful, hateful, deluded, and short-lived,
to be able to cultivate and maintain the precepts and perform various meritorious deeds is truly rare and extraordinary.

Upon hearing this, the practitioner should give rise to joy and practice in accordance with the sutras; they will certainly encounter the three assemblies at the Dragon Flower [Buddha’s] enlightenment. Furthermore, one must first clarify the Tiantai school’s Dharma-gate of the inherent nature (*xingju*). Only then, by practicing based on that nature, will every phenomenon accord with the nature.

Since the essence of the nature is unfathomable, all phenomena are inconceivable. Thus, pouring water and offering flowers become a mass of merit; practicing conditioned goodness is itself the cause for the outflow-free (*anāsrava*). Therefore, it is said that "one is immeasurable and the immeasurable is one," such that a single hair-tip contains world-systems as numerous as kings.

The Wheel of Dharma within the dust is the natural law of reality; it does not rely on supernatural power. It is not only that those of an inherently virtuous nature are thus [liberated], but even those who practice in opposition can achieve liberation. This is why Devadatta was destined to become a Heavenly King. Therefore, our "Mountain School" (Shan-jia) doctrine of the single nature’s inherent possession is forever distinct from all other teachings.

I pray that my fellow practitioners, if advancing, shall be like Sudhana, directly reaching the ocean of Samantabhadra’s practices in a single lifetime; if retreating, they must emulate Yongming, performing the one hundred and eight matters day and night.
Within this very illusory body is the King of Mountains of Merit. Why worry about the Dragon Flower Assembly? One will surely be called a Son of the Buddha.
○ Tenth, the *General Contemplation on Maitreya’s Rebirth Above in Tuṣita* states:
"After fifty-six hundred million years according to the age of Jambudvīpa, he will then descend to be born.
From this, one knows that human life spans are short while Maitreya’s arrival is delayed; if one does not first take birth in the Inner Court, one will ultimately [fail to meet him].

To speak of the Dragon Flower [Buddha] is like seeking the night by looking at the eggs of a bird; how much more so now that we encounter this age of decline (*kṣaya-kalpa*), when our lifespans are as fleeting as mayflies?
Even those who abide before the stage of realization in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) still frequently experience regression, such as Śāriputra.

As for us with our initial resolve, having long dwelt amidst the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), is it not possible that we might stumble and fall? Therefore, we should take the end of our lives as our deadline; as long as there is even a single breath remaining, we must persevere.

You must exert yourself with single-minded diligence and zealously cultivate this Dharma. May you aspire to be reborn in the Pure Land early on, so as to behold the ūrṇā-kośa between the eyebrows and realize the stage of non-retrogression.
There, at the Dragon Flower Assembly, you shall encounter [Maitreya] in the mere snap of a finger. What is called "five hundred and sixty million years" is like the turning of a candlewick;
thus one knows that Tuṣita is a transformation-city for us—is this not fitting? Furthermore, as for the people of this Southern Continent...

Lifespans are indeed short here; yet, it is precisely because of this that those with the faculties of the Mahāyāna gather. If one can apply oneself with diligent cultivation, then samādhi will be easily accomplished and the Great Matter can be fulfilled.
This is not like other regions, where one must pass through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust before the mind finally opens.
Therefore, the devaputras made this vow: "We now take this priceless jewel-pearl celestial crown to offer in worship to the assembly of those with the Great Mind."
Because he has been born [in this way], this person shall before long attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in a future life.
Since Maitreya is thus called a being of great resolve (*mahā-citta*), it is known that those who do not possess such great resolve are unfit to be his retinue.
Therefore, we should broaden our profound minds beyond the six directions of space and dissolve the *dharmadhātu* within the square inch of our hearts. By means of the ocean of birth and death...
It serves as a secure dwelling. Taking the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) as a lamp, one neither perceives a nirvāṇa into which to enter, nor perceives a triple world from which to emerge.
One must be like Sudhana, first generating the vast bodhicitta, and only thereafter beholding the various inconceivable matters within the Vairocana pavilion.
Furthermore, a practitioner who wishes to contemplate Tuṣita should know that regarding that heaven:
These matters of adornment and so forth, though manifested through the power of the vows of five hundred billion devaputras and the Lohitaka spirits,

are entirely accomplished through the illusory-like samādhi of the Buddhas of the ten directions, as well as the mind-only consciousness-concentration and the samādhi of loving-kindness of Maitreya Bodhisattva.
How much more so, then, can the Buddhas of the ten directions and Maitreya Bodhisattva bestow [benefits] upon me?
Contemplate that the mind is of one and the same true reality (*dharmatā*). Therefore, it is said that the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-different in these three respects.
Having understood this, one should then sit cross-legged and contemplate with meticulous attention each of the celestial realms' supreme and wondrous adornments.

This is divided into four parts: first, contemplating the environment (*niśraya-vipāka*); second, contemplating the beings (*sattva-vipāka*); third, contemplating rebirth in the upper realms; and fourth, concluding with the benefits of invoking the Name.

Regarding the first, at the entry into meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there are three types of contemplation through detachment. If the contemplation of the mind is perfected, these three are each mutually complete, like the three legs of a tripod or the three eyes of Maheśvara;
raising one is equivalent to all three. They are neither separate nor conjoined, by means of the wisdom of the true aspect (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*) as taught in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Illuminating each and every thing as the totality of the Dharma-realm—what is called "wisdom of the true aspect" (yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa-jñāna) is precisely the Perfect and Sudden Threefold Calming and Contemplation (samatha-vipaśyanā).
In the teachings of the Mountain School, the contemplation of the ten realms of beings' form and mind all relies upon the Ten Modes of Contemplation.

The first is the contemplation of the inconceivable realm (acintya-vastu), which means contemplating the single moment of deluded mind that presently arises as being fully endowed with the three thousand [dharmas], and as being simultaneously empty, provisional, and the Middle Way.
Second is the genuine arousal of the bodhicitta, which is to arouse the Four Great Vows based upon the sublime object. Third is the skillful settling of the mind in *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*;

that is, to be constantly quiescent while illuminating is called *śamatha*, and to be constantly illuminating while quiescent is called *vipaśyanā*. This is based upon the aforementioned sublime object.

This gives rise to calming and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), which in turn uses wondrous contemplation to illuminate the preceding objects. Fourth is the "Pervasive Destruction of Dharmas" (*dharmavyāptibhañjana*):

"Destruction" refers to the threefold contemplation within a single mind; "dharmas" refers to the three delusions within a single thought-moment. By illuminating them with the perfect contemplation, there is no delusion that is not destroyed. Fifth is "Discerning the Openings and Blockages":

this means that the six hindrances and the three delusions constitute the blockages, while the six perfections and the three contemplations constitute the openings. Sixth is the "Harmonization of the Six Categories," wherein—

The thirty-seven factors of the path of non-action (*asaṃskṛta-mārga*) are entered through balanced cultivation. Seventh, the seven aids for counteracting obstacles that assist the opening [of realization]:

this refers to when one cultivates correct contemplation but encounters many hindrances such that the perfect principle does not open; one must then separately cultivate specific practices to assist it, such as the five stages of settling the mind (*pañca-vinodana-citta*) and the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).

Eighth, knowing the stages and positions: this refers to the six levels of "immediacy" (*liù jí*) and the fifty-five paths to enlightenment (*bodhi-mārga*), through which one clearly understands the degrees of depth and shallowness.

However, this is to avoid the fault of overweening pride (*adhimāna*). Ninth is the ability to practice patience (*kṣānti*): this means that regarding all circumstances, whether adverse or favorable, one remains unmoved in mind;
from the fifth stage, the *wu-pin* (five ranks), one enters the purity of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriyaviśuddhi*). Tenth is the absence of attachment to the Dharma (*dharmatṛṣṇā*):

this means that once practitioners have entered the six faculties and the semblance of principle has become manifest, they must not give rise to craving or attachment, but must proceed directly into the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) to perceive the true principle. As it says:
These ten dharmas are established to accommodate three types of faculties. For a person of the highest of the high faculties, the first alone is sufficient; why would they require the other nine?
Now, observing Tuṣita—whether as provisional or as ultimate—it is inconceivable; therefore, one must observe it with the single mind and the threefold contemplation.
First, the contemplation of the external environment (*niśraya-vipāka*) has two parts. First is the formal contemplation.
The *Sūtra on Maitreya Bodhisattva’s Rebirth Above* states: "At that time, in the Tuṣita Heaven, there were five billion devaputras.
Each and every devaputra had all practiced the profound *dāna-pāramitā* (perfection of giving) in order to make offerings to the One Who is to Succeed to Buddhahood in His Final Birth."
Because they were bodhisattvas, by the power of their celestial merit, they constructed palaces.
Each removed their sandalwood *maṇi* jewel crowns, knelt with palms joined, and made this vow: "I now take these priceless jewels and celestial crowns to offer to this being of great resolve;
in a future life, this person shall before long attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

[They attained] anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. As for me, having received the prediction of enlightenment from that Buddha in that adorned realm, my precious crown was transformed into offering implements.
Then these sons of the gods each knelt on one knee and made great vows.
It was likewise so. When the sons of the gods had made this vow, these jeweled crowns transformed into five hundred trillion jeweled palaces.
Each jeweled palace had seven tiers of walls, each wall being composed of the seven precious gems.
From each wall issued five hundred billion rays of light, and within each ray of light were five hundred billion lotus flowers. Within each [lotus flower]...
From the lotus, five hundred billion rows of trees made of the seven precious gems were manifested.
Each leaf of every tree possessed five hundred billion jewel-colored hues. Within each jewel-colored hue, there were five hundred billion rays of Jāmbūnada gold light.
From within each ray of Jāmbūnada gold light, five hundred billion celestial jewel-women emerged. Each jewel-woman stood beneath a tree, holding a hundred...
Countless billions of jewel necklaces emit exquisite music. Within that music, there is proclaimed the practice of the irreversible wheel of Dharma.
The trees produce fruit the color of crystal; all other colors are absorbed into the color of the crystal.
These rays of light spiral to the right and issue forth myriad sounds, expounding the Dharma of great loving-kindness and great compassion.
Each wall is sixty-two *yojanas* high and fourteen *yojanas* thick.
Five hundred billion dragon kings surround these walls, and each dragon king rains down five hundred billion rows of trees made of the seven treasures, adorning the tops of the walls. From—
However, there is a wind that blows upon these trees, causing them to rub against one another, thereby proclaiming suffering, emptiness, impermanence, non-self, and the various *pāramitās*.

(This is because five hundred billion devaputras practice the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) based on the profound *prajñā*; thus, giving is also called "profound. By the power of this profundity, they are able to transform and create the inner court of Tuṣita;

therefore, every single adornment is beyond measure. Since giving relies upon *prajñā*, it can encompass all the perfections, with each perfection mutually complete. Every dharma is inconceivable. From the devaputras down to the seven-jeweled walking trees, their number is...)

All are five. When this contemplation is perfected, one is able to completely subdue the afflictions of the five stages of dwelling and realize entry into the stage of the five grades of contemplative practice. It is also called the Ground of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*). The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The grasping mind is empty and luminous; it is purely wisdom.

The nature of wisdom is bright and perfect, polishing the ten directions. Is this not practicing the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) by relying on prajñā? It further states: "Having dry wisdom is called the Ground of Dry Wisdom. The habit-energy of desire is initially dried up, yet one has not yet connected with the flow of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-water. Below this, one enters the stage of the Ten Faiths."
At that time, there was a great deity in this palace named Lohitākṣa (Lao-du-bo-ti). He immediately rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions, and made a grand vow:
"If my merit and virtue are sufficient, may I build a Hall of Good Dharma for Maitreya Bodhisattva."
"May there spontaneously emerge from my forehead a jewel.

Having made this vow, there spontaneously emerged from his forehead ten billion precious jewels—lapis lazuli, crystal, and every variety of color, all perfectly complete—like purple-blue *maṇi* gems, transparent throughout both inside and out.
These *maṇi* jewels circled through the air and transformed into forty-nine tiers of subtle and wondrous jeweled palaces.
Each and every balustrade is composed of ten billion *brahma-maṇi* jewels.
Between the various balustrades, nine hundred million *devaputras* and five hundred billion celestial maidens (*devakanyā*) are spontaneously manifested.

In the hand of each *devaputra*, there are manifested immeasurable billions of lotus flowers made of the seven treasures. Upon each lotus flower, there are immeasurable billions of rays of light; within those rays of light...
Equipped with all kinds of musical instruments, such celestial music resounds spontaneously without being struck.

When these sounds emerge, the women naturally take up various instruments and vie with one another to rise for song and dance; the melodies they sing proclaim the ten wholesome actions and the four great vows.
All the devas who heard this gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment. At that time, within the walls there were channels of eight-colored lapis lazuli;
each channel was composed of five hundred billion precious jewels.

Within each channel was water of eight flavors, complete with the eight colors, which surged upward and circled between the beams and rafters. Outside the four gates, four [beings] were born by transformation.
Flowers. Water flows forth from within the flowers like a stream of precious blossoms.

Upon each flower, there are twenty-four celestial maidens whose complexions are subtle and exquisite, their adorned physical forms resembling those of bodhisattvas. From their hands, five hundred billion precious vessels spontaneously manifest;
within each vessel, the various nectars of the heavens naturally overflow. On their left shoulders, they carry and wear immeasurable necklaces.
[The deity] is adorned with necklaces; upon his right shoulder he further carries immeasurable musical instruments.

Like clouds dwelling in the sky, they emerge from the water and praise the Bodhisattva’s six *pāramitās*. [This refers to] Lohitākṣa (Lao-duo-ba-ti), a guardian deity of the palace. Since immeasurable kalpas past, he has long purified his faculties and cultivated supreme merit amidst the subtle six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).

Now, for the sake of Maitreya, he constructs the Hall of Good Dharma (*kuśaladharma-śālā*); therefore, the various six sense-objects within this hall are all exquisitely refined. As for the statement that "pearls emerge from his forehead," it symbolizes that all sense-objects emerge from the unsurpassed Middle Way of the True Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). [One hundred billion...]

Below the precious jewels, reaching up to the immeasurable billions of lights upon the flowers, is the object of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*). Within those lights, reaching to all the gods who hear them and causing them all to resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, is the object of sound (*śabda-viṣaya*).

At that time, within the railings, reaching to the flowing jewel-flowers, is the object of fragrance (*gandha-viṣaya*). Upon each flower, reaching to the nectar of the gods which naturally overflows, is the object of taste (*rasa-viṣaya*). On the left shoulder, bearing immeasurable necklaces, is the object of touch (*spraṣṭavya-viṣaya*). On the right shoulder, again bearing [them] up to the six *pāramitās*, is the object of phenomena (*dharma-viṣaya*).

These six objects have been formed by this deity through long-term perfuming by the *maitrī-citta-samādhi* (samādhi of loving-kindness) of Maitreya; she in turn uses these dharmas to make offerings to the Bodhisattva. If this contemplation is perfected, it is called "Following."

Provisionally entering emptiness through contemplation—namely, the "one emptiness, all emptiness"—one destroys the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), perceives the principle of the True Truth (*satyārtha*), attains all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*), and realizes the stage of the seven levels of faith prior to the ten faiths, wherein the six sense faculties are purified. This is also called the "stage of semblance" (*pratirūpa-bhūmi*).
Because the essence of the principle of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) appears as if manifest, it is nevertheless obscured by the two delusions.
Furthermore, there were great lion thrones made of the seven treasures, four *yojanas* in height, fashioned from Jāmbūnada gold and immeasurable varieties of precious jewels.

These served as adornments. At each of the four corners of the seat, four lotus flowers sprang forth; each lotus flower was composed of a hundred jewels, and from each jewel issued ten billion rays of light.
These lights were subtle and wondrous, transforming into five hundred billion clusters of various precious flowers that adorned the jeweled canopy.
At that time, the hundreds of thousands of Brahma Kings from the ten directions each held a sublime [flower] of the Brahma heavens.
Precious bells were made from jewels and suspended above the jeweled canopy. At that time, the minor Brahma kings held celestial treasures to form a net that completely covered the canopy.
Then, hundreds of thousands of countless sons of gods and their retinues of goddesses each held precious flowers and scattered them upon the seats.
From all these lotus flowers, five hundred billion jewel-women spontaneously emerged, holding [the flowers] in their hands.
White whisks stood in attendance within the inner pavilion, supporting its four corners.

There were four precious pillars, each of which featured hundreds of thousands of multi-storied pavilions, with Brahma-maṇi jewels forming their latticed enclosures. Within the intervals between these pavilions, there were hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens.

Their forms were wondrous beyond compare. Holding musical instruments in their hands, they proclaimed within the sounds of that music: suffering, emptiness, impermanence, non-self, and the various pāramitās.
Such celestial palaces possessed billions of trillions of immeasurable jewel colors; each and every woman [was likewise adorned].
It was also of the same jewel-like color. At that time, immeasurable devas from the ten directions reached the end of their lives and all vowed to be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace.

(This is because the palace deity had long since attained partial realization [of the fruit], yet manifested as dwelling in the provisional [state] to further create a lion throne for Maitreya. The previous Hall of Good Dharma was the place where the Bodhisattva benefited sentient beings; though unmoving, he moves, by virtue of his great compassion.)

That which is accomplished represents the function of initial awakening (*ādikṣānti*). Now, this lion throne is the object upon which the Bodhisattva sits; it moves yet is unmoving, being accomplished through the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), representing the essence of original awakening (*mūlakṣānti*). Thus, initial and original awakening are non-dual.

Therefore, the hall has seats because its substance is able to encompass all things; the seats have canopies because the effect does not depart from the cause. Thus, precious flowers are spread upon the seats, while the exterior is made firm to awaken sentient beings.

Internally, it is supple and self-protective; thus, some suspend precious bells from it and attend upon it with precious maidens. If its manifestation is directed toward universal salvation, it becomes the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa-citta*). This is why it stands four *yojanas* high, and why at each of its four corners there are four lotus flowers.

If its fulfillment is directed toward the internal domain, it becomes the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses. This is why the number of Brahma kings, sons of gods, and goddesses all totals hundreds of thousands. All of these are the products of the illusory transformations of this deity’s wondrous power of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-māyā-bala*).
When this contemplation is perfected, one enters and realizes the eighth and ninth stages of faith.
At that time, in the Tuṣita Heaven palace, there were five great deities. The first great deity was named Ratnaketu (Jewel Banner);
from his body rained down the seven treasures, which were scattered within the palace walls. Each and every jewel transformed into immeasurable musical instruments, suspended in mid-air;

they resounded spontaneously without being struck, producing immeasurable sounds that accorded with the inclinations of all beings. The second great deity was named Puṣpashrī (Flower Virtue). From his body...
A rain of various flowers fell, completely covering the palace walls and transforming into precious canopies.
Each flower-canopy was preceded by hundreds of thousands of banners and streamers as guides. The third great deity was named Gandharva;

from the pores of his body issued the subtle and wondrous scent of sāgara-tīra-candana, which formed clouds of fragrance in the colors of a hundred jewels, circling the palace seven times. The fourth great deity...
It is named Joyful Delight. It rains wish-fulfilling jewels, each of which naturally rests atop banners and streamers.

They clearly proclaim the immeasurable taking of refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, as well as the five precepts, immeasurable wholesome dharmas, and the pāramitās—sounds that benefit and encourage those seeking awakening.
The fifth great deity is named Right Sound; his body...
From all his pores flowed forth various waters; upon each stream were five hundred billion flowers, and upon each flower were twenty-five jade maidens.
From every pore on the bodies of each jade maiden issued forth all manner of sounds, surpassing all the music of the celestial queens of Māra.

(Beyond this Hall of Good Dharma, there are five great deities. Together with the aforementioned celestial son and the palace deity, these are all the retinue of Maitreya who share his same practices and vows. Having long since realized the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), they have all attained the *māyopama-samādhi* (the samādhi of being like an illusion); therefore, they manifest transformations with sovereign ease.

While the former deities emit pearls from their foreheads, from which ritual implements emerge, these five deities rain down ornaments from their entire bodies and every pore. They are able to make offerings above to the Bodhisattva and bestow benefit below upon sentient beings; thus, they are preeminent. This represents how, from within a single substantial reality, the merits of the fivefold Dharma-body flow forth.

If this contemplation is perfected, it is called "contemplating from emptiness into the provisional" (*kong ru jia guan*). Within one provisional [reality], all are provisional; one destroys the delusions as numerous as fine dust (*rajas*), perceives the principle of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and attains the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*)."

The realization of the fulfillment of the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*) is collectively termed the stage of semblance (*sadr̥śa-bhūmi*). Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*) enters the fulfillment of the ten levels of faith, they are able to shatter the first portion of the ignorance of cessation-characteristics (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*) and enter the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*), wherein the eightfold manifestation of the Way (*aṣṭa-lakṣaṇa-mārga-saṃbodhi*) is achieved.

Thus, one knows that the tenth level of faith is the cause of the first dwelling, and the first dwelling is the fruit of the tenth level of faith. This so-called shattering of the forty-two grades of ignorance begins from the tenth level of faith. There are those who are not conversant with the Tiantai school [who may hold otherwise].

The path of destroying delusions to reveal principle consists of forty-two stages, which are assigned to forty-two positions. To then claim that destroying one grade of ignorance constitutes the first abode (prathamā-bhūmi), and yet—when calculating up to the stage of wondrous enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi)—there still remains one grade that must be explained away in a convoluted manner—is this not erroneous?
Second, the conclusion:
This is named Tuṣita Heaven, a place of supreme and wondrous merit that is the karmic retribution for the ten wholesome deeds.

Furthermore, if there are bhikṣus or any of the great assembly who do not weary of birth and death, who delight in being born in heaven, and who cherish and respect the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta), [they should go there].
Those who wish to become disciples of Maitreya should practice this contemplation. They should contemplate each and every aspect of the exquisite and sublime bliss of Tuṣita Heaven.
One who practices this contemplation is said to have right contemplation (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). If one contemplates otherwise, it is called wrong contemplation (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

(The practitioner must ensure that the object of contemplation is vividly clear, whether with eyes open or closed, exactly as described in the sūtras; this is called right contemplation. Beyond this, not only is what shown by non-Buddhists and those of the Lesser Vehicle called wrong, but even [the views of] all the Great [Vehicle... )

According to the teachings of the *Sūtras*, that which does not accord with this scripture is likewise called "false. If, while in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one suddenly sees a Buddha-land in another direction that surpasses Tuṣita, there are two possibilities:

First, it may be that although the practitioner has previously cultivated the contemplation of the Buddha-recollection (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*) in past lives but has not yet perfected it, it manifests momentarily through the power of those latent roots. In such a case, one should simply focus single-mindedly on the name of Maitreya Bodhisattva’s great compassion and direct one's contemplation toward Tuṣita; then, by the compassionate power of all Buddhas, one will be able to assist one's correct contemplation and will surely achieve success quickly.

Second, it may be that in past lives one practiced heterodox paths, and the seeds of these false thoughts now reside within the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*). Now, due to the pressure of the power of correct contemplation, these false seeds arise from within, and the Māra Pāpīyān seizes this opportunity.

Therefore, they transform the Buddha-land to delude the practitioner. One should counteract this with the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). To counteract these phenomena, one should reflect for oneself that all dharmas are merely manifestations of the mind. Since my own mind is empty, quiescent, and without a master—being like the single true mark (*tathatā*)—from where could various objects arise?

Furthermore, objects do not exist as objects of their own accord; they are objects because of the mind. The mind does not exist as mind of its own accord; it exists as mind because of objects. Now, when I seek the mind, it is utterly unobtainable; how then can there be any objects? When reflecting in this way, if it is indeed a Buddha-realm, it will become increasingly clear and sublime;

one should treat it according to the method previously described. If it is a manifestation of Māra, in light cases it will immediately vanish. In heavy cases, it undergoes various shifts and changes, being unstable—sometimes good, sometimes evil; sometimes joyful, sometimes sorrowful. The practitioner, with a single-minded focus...

Focus your mind on right contemplation and the essence of the true mark (*dharmatā*). Pay homage universally to all Buddhas, diligently perform the five repentances, and recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*. Before long, [the obstacle] will naturally dissipate and perish, unable to cause harm. Furthermore, now contemplate Tuṣita.

Even the sudden vision of images such as those at Longhua is not yet correct contemplation; it must also be relinquished. How much more so for other dharmas that one might find attractive and cling to? Should even a slight attachment arise, one will inevitably join the ranks of the heterodox, destroying right knowledge and insight, and fail to be of the lineage of the Dharma King. How can one not be cautious in this regard?

II. Contemplating the Primary Retribution (which consists of two types: the noble and the ordinary. First is the *pariṇāmanika-kāya* [transformation body], which is manifested through the perfuming of the samādhi of noble ones beyond the realms.

Second is the *āntarābhava-kāya* [segmentary body], which is the retribution-body obtained through the power of karma of ordinary beings within the realms. Now, Tuṣita Heaven possesses both of these types. In the Inner Court, all are the abodes of non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas; therefore, the bodies of the devaputras and devakanyās there are transformation bodies.

In the Outer Court, they are purely ordinary devas; their bodies are segmentary. Maitreya also manifests two kinds of bodies: being born in the village of Kapila in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī into the family of the Brahmin Pāpali, this demonstrates his identity with the segmentary body. As for Śākyamuni...)

After preaching the *Sūtra on Rebirth Above*, he entered parinirvāṇa on the fifteenth day of the second month in the twelfth year. He was immediately reborn by transformation in this very heaven; this demonstrates that his body was identical to the *pariṇāmika-kāya* (body of transformation). Practitioners should contemplate that the bodhisattva’s body of transformation is itself the *dharmakāya*.

How much more so for that which is not the *saṃbhogakāya*. Since one has already attained the non-duality of emptiness and the conventional, and the simultaneous fusion of the ultimate and the mundane, through the preceding contemplations, and has realized the stage of the fulfillment of the ten faiths, one should now exclusively employ the wondrous contemplation of the Middle Way to contemplate the primary retribution (*prātibhāsika-śarīra*) of Maitreya, thereby entering the stage of partial realization.
At that time, within the seven-jeweled terrace of the Tuṣita Heaven, upon a lion throne in a maṇi palace, he was suddenly born by transformation.
He sat cross-legged upon a lotus flower, his body the color of Jāmbūnada gold, sixteen yojanas in height, fully endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
Upon the crown of his head was the uṣṇīṣa, and his hair was deep blue like lapis lazuli.
[The crown] was of lapis lazuli color. It was adorned with Śakrābhilagna-maṇis and hundreds of thousands of millions of bījaka-jewels.

It possessed hundreds of thousands of millions of colors, and within each color were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of transformation Buddhas, with various transformed Bodhisattvas serving as their attendants.
Furthermore, there were great Bodhisattvas from other directions who performed the eighteen transformations at will.
He was present, dwelling within a celestial crown. From the white tuft of hair between Maitreya’s eyebrows, light radiated forth, manifesting in the colors of a hundred jewels.

Within each of his thirty-two marks, there were five hundred billion jewel-colored hues; likewise, within each of his secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*), there were also five hundred billion jewel-colored hues.
From each mark and secondary characteristic, eighty-four thousand clouds of radiant light issued forth in splendor, together with all...
The sons of heaven each sat upon lotus thrones, and throughout the six periods of day and night, they constantly expounded the practice of the Dharma-wheel of the stage of non-retrogression.
Within a single period, they brought five hundred billion sons of heaven to fulfillment, causing them not to retrogress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Thus, while dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven, they constantly expound this stage of non-retrogression day and night.
The Wheel of Dharma. He delivers all the devaputras. (This is Maitreya Bodhisattva;

since he first resolved his mind on *bodhicitta* following his own name-stage, three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and one hundred *kalpas* have passed. This is his final body at the culmination of the causal stage. Therefore, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni bestowed upon him the prediction that he would attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in one more lifetime.

Having been reborn above from this heaven, he shall remain for five billion six hundred million years in Jambudvīpa before descending to be born below. Some say that eight hundred and eighty thousand nine thousand three hundred years after the parinirvāṇa of Śākyamuni, Maitreya...)

Regarding the Buddha’s appearance in the world: if one follows the latter calculation, the former is short by three million two hundred and nine thousand three hundred years. The former was spoken from the Golden Mouth [of the Buddha], while the latter is a *koṭi*-based reckoning; it is unknown which is correct. His ascent to Tuṣita is to gather the disciples of Śākyamuni during the final dharma (*mappō*);

his descent to Jambudvīpa is to transform those sentient beings whose capacities for the Three Vehicles have matured. This, too, accords with the expedient means (*upāya*) of the *siddhānta*. Moreover, since Maitreya’s supernatural powers are vast and his wondrous functions are inconceivable, even before his ascent to Tuṣita—moment by moment, in every atom—when has he not attained perfect enlightenment?

Where has he not manifested the eight phases of birth to deliver sentient beings? He shares the same Dharma-body and the same ultimate realization as all Buddhas of the three periods; who is superior and who inferior? Who is earlier and who is later?

Which comes first? The conditions for this land will follow later; therefore, it is said that seeking fame is not as good as [the path of] Gautama. Fearing that the capacities of those in other lands may ripen, it might yet be that Śākyamuni is not as good as Maitreya—this cannot be known.

Thus, we know that the discourse on "delighting in wandering among secular clans" and the statement regarding "that which develops first but is perfected later" do no more than exalt and humble his Way to encourage future generations. This is merely like a phantom person speaking in a dream. According to the teachings of the vehicles, he truly corresponds to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) and the Diamond Dry Wisdom (*vajra-śuṣka-prajñā*). It is also called the "Final Mind of the Diamond.

Having already traversed the twelve stages of single and double progression in their manifold layers, he is about to enter the ocean of the fruit of Wondrous Enlightenment (*tathāgata-phala-sāgara*). As for the practitioner: having previously observed the dependent retribution and thereby destroyed the secondary afflictions (*kleśa*), they now observe the primary retribution, precisely to destroy the [afflictions of] birth and abiding.

When this contemplation is perfected—namely, the contemplation of the non-duality of emptiness and the provisional—it is called the "Contemplation of the Non-duality of Emptiness and Provisionality. This means that within one [aspect], all are included. By destroying one grade and extinguishing the afflictions of the characteristic of cessation, one first enters the stage of partial realization, the First Abode (*prathamā-bhūmi*). Within the secret treasury of the three virtues, one perceives a portion of the *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect wisdom). Because fundamental ignorance has been first destroyed and the principle of the Truths has first manifested, one obtains a partial vision of the adornments of the marks and signs of the Stage of Near-Enlightenment (*upapatti-sthāna*). Having already joined the stream of the sages, one realizes the stage of non-retrogression. Question: In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, even at the Eighth Ground one still requires the seven exhortations of the Tathāgata; it is only at the Seventh Abode of the Perfect Teaching that one first receives the name of "non-retrogression. How can it be so immediately at the First Abode? Answer: Indeed, the term "retrogression" applies only up to the stage of faith (*śraddhā*). At the First Abode, one has already transcended the stage of faith and entered the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Therefore, there is no retrogression. Furthermore, the principle of the Three Truths is fully present within a single grade; thus, when one grade is destroyed, all grades are simultaneously destroyed. Consequently, the power of non-retrogression is attained from the very beginning. Moreover, the *Avataṃsaka* speaks of the Eighth Ground because it is based on the common teaching (*pāramitā-naya*), whereas the Perfect Teaching is based on the distinct teaching (*viśeṣa-naya*). Since the two teachings differ, their stages do not correspond. Therefore, the meaning of non-retrogression is established from the First Abode onward. As for the statement that one must wait until the Seventh Abode to attain the name of non-retrogression, this refers to the specific terminology used in the *Avataṃsaka*. However, in the Perfect Teaching, the name of non-retrogression is applied from the First Abode. Thus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, regarding the statement that one must wait for the seven exhortations of the Tathāgata, this refers to the fact that at the Eighth Ground, although one has realized the principle of the Middle Way, one has not yet fully severed the subtle habits of ignorance. Therefore, one must receive the seven exhortations to further sever these habits and manifest the fruit of Buddhahood. When Maitreya Tathāgata appears in the world, it will be precisely at the juncture when the period of increase has reached its peak and the period of decrease has just begun.

Consequently, the excellence of his realm and the longevity of his body and lifespan will be identical to those of the pure lands of all Buddhas; this should especially be understood by dividing them into the four types of lands.
Only when one’s virtue is fully perfected can this be achieved; otherwise, principle and phenomena will become confounded, and essence and function will be indiscriminately mixed.

If so, from where can one observe the mind? The true reality (dharmatā) will remain unmanifest. Thus, delusion originates with principle, while awakening must begin with phenomena. Truly, although one speaks of sudden cultivation, it does not preclude gradual attainment.

Regarding what are called the four lands: the first is the Land of Common Dwelling for Ordinary Beings and Sages. This is the realm inhabited by those of the seven destinies, including devas and humans, as well as the śrāvakas of the *piṭaka* (Tripitaka) teaching.
The Buddha-body perceived therein is the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) that achieves enlightenment through the eight phases.

It is also called the "birth-body. It possesses the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs; according to the sutras, its height is sometimes said to be one thousand *chi* (cubits), and sometimes sixteen *zhang*.
Some say it is eighty *zhǔ*; this is correct. Although the environments they inhabit may be either defiled or pure, they share this same Great Trichiliocosm and these same sun and moon.

If this were not so, why would there still be three ailments at that time—namely, (1) food and drink, (2) excrement and urine, and (3) aging? Second is the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder (*upāya-śeṣa-bhūmi*);

it consists purely of those of the One Vehicle according to the Shared Teaching (*samānīta-yāna*) and is the dwelling place of Bodhisattvas. What they perceive is the physical body (*janma-kāya*) of the Honored One.

Specifically, those who have realized the emptiness-only of the Two Vehicles perceive the *saṃbhoga-kāya* (the body born of parents), while Bodhisattvas who have realized non-emptiness perceive the *vairocana-kāya* (the special, exalted body).

Since there are thus two types of Buddha-bodies, how could their lands be one? (The former corresponds to the "shared" [tongju] realm, and the latter to the "recompensed" [shibao] realm. Third is the Realm of Real Reward Adornment (*sambhoga-vyuha-kṣetra*).

This is the dwelling place of the Bodhisattvas of the Separate and Perfect Teachings, whom the followers of the Two Vehicles are unable to see. What they perceive is only the *vairocana* (exalted) body;

this body possesses immeasurable colors, each color possesses immeasurable marks, and each mark possesses immeasurable secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*). The environment upon which it rests and its retributive rewards likewise possess immeasurable varieties of adornment.
According to what is manifested, these are boundless and inexhaustible, just as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

It is said that each of the Buddha’s marks and signs of excellence (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) contains as many [subtle features] as there are atoms in ten *kusumagarbha* worlds. Fourth is the Land of Constant Quiescent Light (*nityapraśāntaprakāśa-kṣetra*).

This is the ultimate stage of fruition of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and three periods of time; it is the dwelling place of the pure *dharmakāya*. Its form is equal to the great void, and its essence is the *dharmadhātu*.
It is realized only by Buddhas and is not the domain of Bodhisattvas. Even those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) in the Perfect Teaching (*paripūrṇayāna*)...
If this is not yet fully understood, how much less so for those below the [first] stage?
Such a classification not only reveals that the Sages possess the power to manifest forms in response to sentient beings, but also opens a gateway for practitioners to cultivate their practice.

Thus we know that although the Lotus Forest of Kukkutapāda is said to be pure and superior, compared to the present five turbidities, it is nothing more than a place where merit is abundant and faculties are sharp. It is therefore appropriate that we dwell together here.
First, a brief indication of the city walls. The *Sūtra on the Descent of Maitreya Bodhisattva* states:

"In this realm, there shall be a city named Kukkuṭa (Chicken Head). It is twelve yojanas from east to west and seven yojanas from north to south" (the *Sūtra on Maitreya’s Attainment of Buddhahood* states:

"There is a great city named Ketumatī, one thousand two hundred yojanas in length and breadth, and seven yojanas in height"). The land is fertile and abundant, the population is flourishing, and the streets—

The alleys formed into rows (naturally manifested seven-jeweled pavilions, majestic and exquisite, adorned and pure. Within the windows and doors stood various jeweled maidens, each holding in her hand a net of pearls, decorated with miscellaneous jewels to cover them above;

precious bells were suspended closely together, their sounds like celestial music. Seven-jeweled rows of trees stood between which were canals and springs, all made of the seven jewels; they flowed with waters of different colors, reflecting one another, meandering and gliding across each other without obstruction.
On both its banks, pure golden sand was spread. The streets, lanes, and thoroughfares were twelve *li* wide and entirely pure, like a celestial garden adorned with various jewels.

At that time, there was a dragon king in the city named Jala-prabha (Water-Light), who rained down fragrant moisture at night and was clear and harmonious during the day. There was also a great dragon king named Tālaśikhin, fully endowed with merit and majestic power.

Near the city, the palace of this dragon king appeared outside like a tower made of the seven treasures; it would constantly manifest at midnight in human form, using an auspicious vase filled with fragrant-colored water to sprinkle and settle the dust, moistening the ground.

It was like a coating of oil; as people traveled back and forth, there was no dust or grime. This was due to the merit of the people of that time. At every intersection of the streets and lanes stood pillars of great luminous pearls, twelve *li* high, their radiance surpassing that of the sun.

Each illuminated eighty *yojanas* in the four directions. They were of pure golden hue, and their brilliance shone day and night without distinction. The light of lamps and candles was like a heap of ink by comparison. Fragrant winds blew from time to time, blowing upon the pearl pillars and raining down jeweled necklaces, which all the people used for their adornment.

Furthermore, as in the bliss of the third dhyāna, there were everywhere heaps of gold, silver, rare treasures, and clusters of maṇi jewels piled up to form mountains that emitted light shining everywhere. When the people within the city encountered these, they all rejoiced and gave rise to the bodhicitta.
At that time, in the city of Kukkuṭa, there was a rākṣasa named Parṇaśabara who acted in accordance with the Dharma and did not contravene the true teaching.
Every time he waited until the people had fallen asleep, he would remove filth, impurities, and all that was unclean, and furthermore, with incense...

[He] sprinkles the ground with [fragrant] liquid, making it exceedingly fragrant and pure. (There is a great yakṣa deity named Bhadrapāla-saikya who protects the city of Ketumatī and its inhabitants day and night, sweeping and sprinkling them to keep them clean.)
II. A Universal Survey of Jambudvīpa, in three parts: first, the world; second, the people; third, the kings. Now, for the first part:
at that time, the land of Jambudvīpa extended ten thousand *yojanas* from east to west and south to north. All its mountains, rivers, and rocky cliffs were spontaneously extinguished.
The waters of the four great oceans each occupied their respective quarters. At that time, the land of Jambudvīpa was utterly...

It became level and even, as clear and bright as a mirror. (The waters of the four great oceans each decreased by two thousand yojanas. At that time, the land of Jambudvīpa was exactly ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth;
its ground was smooth and pure, like a mirror of lapis lazuli. Throughout the interior of Jambudvīpa, grain was abundant and cheap, the population flourished, and there were many precious jewels.
In all the villages and settlements, the crowing of roosters reached one another. These wretched trees of flowers and fruit—withered, parched, and foul—also vanished of their own accord.
As for the remaining trees of sweet fruit, whose fragrances were exceptionally fine, they all sprang forth from the earth: great *mahā-manojña* flowers and *mano-rati-kara* flowers.

There are flowers of supreme great sound, *utpala* flowers, flowers of great golden fruit, flowers of seven-jeweled fruit, and flowers of silver fruit. Their filaments are soft and supple, resembling celestial silks; they produce auspicious fruits that are endowed with both fragrance and flavor, as soft as celestial silks.

The flowers of the groves and trees have sweet and exquisite fruits that are exceedingly lush and flourishing, surpassing even the pleasure gardens of Śakra. These trees are tall and prominent, reaching thirty *li* in height, with cities and towns standing so close together that a rooster could fly from one to the next.
Next, one contemplates the people:

at that time, the seasonal climate is harmonious and appropriate, and the four seasons follow their proper order. Within the bodies of these people, there are no afflictions of the one hundred and eight [delusions].
Greed, anger, and ignorance are not particularly intense. The minds of people are even and balanced; they are all of one mind, and when they see one another, they rejoice.
They were joyful and addressed one another with kind words; their speech was of a single type, without any distinction, just like that of the people of Uttarakuru, and no different from them.
At that time, within Jambudvīpa, the people—both great and small—all shared a single resonance, with no diversity or difference whatsoever.
At that time, when men and women desired to relieve themselves, the earth would naturally [provide for them].
When it was opened, after the task was completed, the ground closed back together as before. At that time, non-glutinous rice grew naturally upon Jambudvīpa;
it had no husks and was exceedingly fragrant and delicious. Eating it caused no affliction or suffering.

Furthermore, gold, silver, precious gems, conch shells, agate, pearls, and amber were scattered everywhere on the ground, yet no one took note of them. At that time, the people held these in their hands.
The jewels said to one another: "In the past, because of these very jewels, people harmed one another, were imprisoned in jails, and underwent countless sufferings and afflictions.
Now, these jewels are treated no differently than tiles and stones, with no one to guard them.
At that time, within Jambudvīpa, garments grew spontaneously upon trees—extremely fine and soft—which people would gather and wear, just as they do now.

The people of Uttarakuru have garments that grow spontaneously upon trees, and there is nothing else; this is entirely due to the great roots of goodness they planted under the present Buddha and the retribution for their practice of a compassionate mind.

Those born in that land possess innate wisdom and majestic virtue; they enjoy the manifold requisites of the five desires, happiness, and tranquility. Furthermore, there are no ailments caused by cold, heat, wind, or fire, nor do they suffer the nine types of afflictions.

Their lifespan is full, reaching eighty-four thousand years, and none meet with untimely death. The human body is sixteen *zhang* tall, and day after day they experience supreme and exquisite peace and joy. They take deep meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) as their instrument of delight. There are only three kinds of illness: first, eating and drinking; second, excretion; and third, aging. As for women, at the age of five...

Only at the age of one hundred would they marry. Should they have any bodily excretions, the earth would crack open to receive them; once received, it would close back up, and red lotuses would grow there to cover the foul odor. At that time, when the people of the world grew old and decrepit, they would naturally go to the mountains and forests to dwell beneath the trees.

In peace and tranquility, they will bring their mindfulness of the Buddha to completion and pass away. They will mostly be reborn in the Great Brahma Heaven or before the various Buddhas. Those lands will be secure and peaceful, free from enemies, bandits, or the calamities of robbery. In the cities and villages, no one shall have to close their doors.

Furthermore, there will be no suffering from old age, nor the perils of water, fire, weapons, famine, or poison. People will always possess hearts of loving-kindness, being respectful and harmonious; they will subdue their sense faculties as a son obeys his father or as a mother cherishes her child. Their speech will be humble and modest—all this is due to Maitreya.

They were trained through a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and maintained the precept against killing because they did not eat meat. By virtue of these causes and conditions, those born in that land have tranquil faculties, upright countenances, and are endowed with majestic marks like celestial youths.

Furthermore, there are eighty-four thousand small cities made of various jewels as its retinue, with the city of Ketumatī situated at its center. Whether men or women, old or young, far or near, they are all able to see one another without obstruction due to the Buddha’s spiritual power, like *maṇi* gems that emit light at night and fulfill wishes.

Pearl blossoms fill the world. At that time, throughout Jambudvīpa, there is always a fine fragrance, like that of the Fragrant Mountain (Gandhamādana). The flowing waters are beautiful, their taste sweet and capable of removing afflictions. Rain falls in due season, and the celestial gardens ripen with fragrant and exquisite varieties of rice.

By the power of the devas, a single sowing yields seven harvests with very little labor and a vast yield. The grain grows luxuriantly, free from weeds and chaff. Through the merit of sentient beings and the karmic fruition of their past deeds, food enters the mouth and is digested;
it possesses a hundred flavors, incomparably fragrant and delicious, and fills one with strength.
Third, regarding the observation of the king:
At that time, a Dharma King appeared named Śaṅkha. He ruled and transformed the world through the True Dharma, and the seven treasures were perfected.

As for these so-called seven treasures, they are: the precious golden wheel, the precious elephant, the precious horse, the precious jewel, the precious queen, the precious minister of war, and the precious treasurer.
These are called the seven treasures, which stabilize this land of Jambudvīpa; without the use of weapons or force, all naturally submit.
Among the four treasuries of jewels, the first is the country of Gandhāra, the Airāvata Treasure Store, which contains immeasurable quantities of various rare gems and extraordinary objects.
The second is the country of Mithilā, the Pañcāla Great Treasury, which likewise abounds in rare jewels. The third is the country of... [Su-]... [text fragment ends].
In the great kingdom of Rāṣṭrapāla, there is a great treasure trove, abounding in rare jewels.

Fourthly, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there is the great treasure trove of Śaṅkha, likewise filled with many rare jewels beyond measure or calculation. These four great treasuries manifest spontaneously.
The various treasury keepers each came and said to the king, "We pray only that Your Majesty will bestow these treasures from the storehouse upon the poor.
At that time, Great King Śaṅkha, having obtained these treasures, likewise did not take account of them and ultimately had no thought of them as material wealth.

(At that time, there was a Wheel-Turning Sage King in that land named Śaṅkha. He possessed the fourfold army and governed the four continents without relying on military force. He was endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. The King...

He has a thousand sons, valiant and handsome, who naturally subdue all enemies. The king possesses seven treasures: first, the golden wheel treasure, with its thousand spokes, hub, and rim, all perfectly complete; second, the elephant treasure, white as the snow mountains, with its seven limbs touching the ground, majestic and beautiful to behold, like a king of mountains;

third, the dark-blue horse treasure, with crimson mane, tail, and hair, flowers blooming beneath its hooves, and hooves and hoofs made of the seven treasures; fourth, the divine jewel treasure, brilliant and beautiful to behold, three cubits in length, raining down jewels from its radiance to fulfill the wishes of sentient beings; fifth...

The Woman-Jewel: her complexion is exquisite and beautiful; she is supple and boneless. The Six Ministers of the Treasury: from their mouths they emit jewels; from beneath their feet rain falls as jewels; from their hands jewels emerge. The Seventh Minister, the Commander-in-Chief: whenever he simply moves his body, the fourfold army emerges from the sky like clouds.

He has a thousand sons. Within his realm, which possesses the seven treasures, all the people look upon one another without harboring ill will, loving each other as a mother loves her child. There are four great treasuries, each surrounded by four hundred million smaller treasuries. These four great treasuries spontaneously open up, manifesting a great radiance;

they are exactly one thousand yojanas in length and breadth, filled with precious jewels, and are each guarded by four great nāgas. These four great treasuries and the various smaller treasuries emerge spontaneously, their forms like lotus flowers. They are without...

Hundreds of people all went together to observe it. At that time, the various jewels had no guardians; when the multitude saw them, their minds felt no attachment, and they cast them upon the ground as if they were tiles, stones, grass, wood, or clods of earth.

Those who saw them at that time felt a sense of weary detachment and said to one another: "As the Buddha has taught, in the past sentient beings, for the sake of these jewels, harmed one another, stole from and plundered each other, and practiced deception and falsehood, causing the offenses of birth and death to increase ever further until they fell into the great hells."
II. Contemplating the Inferior Response Body (*hīna-nirmāṇakāya*) has eight aspects: 1. Descending from Tuṣita; 2. Entering the womb;
3. Abiding in the womb; 4. Emerging from the womb; 5. Leaving home; 6. Subduing Māra and attaining enlightenment (counted as one); 7. Turning the wheel of Dharma; 8. Entering nirvana.
These are called the Eight Aspects of Attaining Enlightenment in the Mahāyāna. If according to the Hīnayāna sūtras, there is no "abiding in the womb," and [the sequence] is combined differently.
Regarding the entry into the womb, they are of one kind. Furthermore, Mahāyāna practitioners see the marks of the Tathāgata as mutually complete, each possessing eight;
Hīnayāna practitioners see the marks as distinct and separate, totaling only eight from beginning to end. Within this, there are two further stages: first, observing the parents.
At that time, that king had a minister named Sūṣma. He was a childhood friend of the king, whom the king deeply loved and respected.
Furthermore, his appearance was handsome: he was neither tall nor short, neither fat nor thin, and neither too pale nor too dark.
He was neither old nor young. At that time, Bimbisāra had a wife named Vaidehī, who was the most exceptionally beautiful among all women, like the consort of the Lord of Devas.
Her mouth emitted the fragrance of the *utpala* lotus, and her body the fragrance of sandalwood.
She was entirely devoid of the eighty-four feminine affectations; she also possessed no illness or thoughts of distracted conceptualization.
Next, regarding the first [section] of the correct contemplation of the Buddha’s body: Descent from Tuṣita.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, while in the Tuṣita Heaven, observed his parents to be neither too old nor too young, and thus descended his spirit to manifest in response.

(At that time, there was a great Brahmin leader in the city named Śuddhama; the Brahmin woman was named Brahmāvatī, whose nature was gentle and compliant. Maitreya took birth with them as his parents. Although they were dwelling [in such a state],...
Entering the womb is like wandering through a celestial palace; emitting great radiance, it is not obstructed by dust or defilement.
(In Dharmarakṣa’s translation, the two stages of entering and dwelling in the womb are missing; here, Kumārajīva’s translation provides them.
Fourth, as for emerging from the womb, he is born from the right side, no different from my own birth today from my right flank. Maitreya Bodhisattva shall be exactly the same.
The various devas of Tuṣita each proclaimed: "Maitreya Bodhisattva has already descended into a womb.
At that time, King Śuddhodana immediately gave his son a name, calling him Maitreya. Maitreya Bodhisattva was adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics;
his body was the color of gold (or the color of purple gold), endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man, and he sat upon a precious lotus flower. Sentient beings...

Beholding him, one never tires; his radiance is so brilliant as to be beyond calculation. It is something never before seen by gods or men. His physical strength is immeasurable; the power of each and every joint universally surpasses that of all mighty dragons and elephants, being truly inconceivable.

The radiance from his pores shines forth immeasurably and without obstruction; the light of the sun, moon, stars, water, fire, and jewels all becomes invisible, appearing like mere dust. His body is eighty cubits tall, and his chest is twenty-five cubits broad.

His face was twelve and a half cubits long; his nose was high, well-formed, and straight, positioned directly at the center of the face. His physical marks were complete, and he was peerlessly handsome, endowed with the primary characteristics and secondary signs of excellence. Each primary characteristic was adorned with eighty-four thousand secondary signs, as if he were a statue cast in pure gold.

From each and every mark of excellence, light radiates forth, illuminating a thousand *yojanas*. His fleshly eye is clear and penetrating; blue and white are distinct. A constant halo of light encircles his body for a hundred *yojanas*, making the sun, moon, stars, pearls, *maṇi* gems, and rows of trees made of the seven treasures all appear bright and radiant within the Buddha’s light.
All other lights lose their utility. The Buddha’s body is tall and majestic, like a mountain of yellow gold. Those who see him naturally escape the three evil realms.

○ Fifth, Leaving Home: At that time, Maitreya was still a householder. Before long, he was to leave home and study the Way. (At that time, Maitreya clearly contemplated the faults and afflictions of the five desires of the world.

He saw sentient beings suffering, submerged in the long-flowing stream, deep within the great cycle of birth and death—truly pitiable. With such right mindfulness, he observed suffering, emptiness, and impermanence; he took no pleasure in the household life and grew weary of the confinement of the home, as if...)

At that time, King Śaṅkha, together with his various ministers, the people of the land, and the citizens, brought forth a palanquin made of the seven treasures, equipped with a thousand jeweled canopies, a thousand jeweled awnings, ten billion jeweled bells, ten billion jeweled banners, a thousand jeweled vessels, and a thousand jeweled jars.

He offered it to Maitreya. Having accepted it, Maitreya gave it away to the brahmins. Once the brahmins had received it, they immediately destroyed it and divided it among themselves. Observing that Maitreya was capable of performing such a great act of giving, the brahmins conceived a sense of wonder.

Seeing this jeweled pavilion vanish in an instant, the Bodhisattva Maitreya realized that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are subject to decay and destruction. Cultivating the perception of impermanence, he recited the verses on impermanence—the cool nectar of the Buddhas of the past:
"All conditioned things are impermanent; this is the law of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased, nirvāṇa is bliss."*
Sixth, the Attainment of Enlightenment:
At that time, not far from the city of Kukkuṭapāda, there was a tree of enlightenment named Nāgapuṣpa, one yojana in height and five hundred paces in breadth.
Thereupon, Maitreya Bodhisattva sat beneath that tree and attained the fruit of unsurpassed enlightenment during that very night.
On that very night that Upatiṣya left the household life, he attained the unsurpassed path. At that moment, the three-thousandfold world system shook in six ways.
The earth deities each announced to one another, "Maitreya has already perfected the Buddha-way.
That sound spread on and reached the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings. It further spread until it was heard throughout the [Heaven of] the Thirty-three.

The three heavens: the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven (these are the various devaputras of the outer court; if those in the inner court hear the Dharma of Non-retrogression, they shall all descend to birth together with Maitreya.

Although those in the outer court dwell in this same heaven as Maitreya, they merely hear his name but do not see his physical form, nor do they hear the Dharma, much less know the signs such as the Bodhisattva’s descent of spirit and entry into the womb. Therefore, at the time of his present attainment of enlightenment, it is by relying on the retribution of the lower heavens that they hear it and only then come to know).
The Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, and even up to the Brahmā Heaven (sitting in the Vajra-adorned site of enlightenment beneath the Dragon-flower Bodhi tree).

The branches are like precious dragons, spitting forth flowers made of a hundred jewels. Each flower and petal displays the colors of the seven treasures, with each color producing a different fruit that accords with the inclinations of sentient beings. Among the heavens and the human realm, there is nothing to compare with it. The tree is fifty yojanas high, its branches and leaves spreading out in the four directions.

He emitted a great radiance. At that time, Maitreya, together with eighty-four thousand Brahmins, went to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Maitreya immediately shaved his head, left the household life, and began to study the Way. Having left home early in the morning, on the very first watch of that night, he subdued the four kinds of Māras and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

He then spoke this verse: "For a long time I have contemplated the suffering of sentient beings, wishing to pull them out, yet finding no way to liberate them. Now that I have realized Bodhi, all things are suddenly seen as non-existent. I have also penetrated the emptiness of sentient beings;

their fundamental nature and characteristics are as they truly are. Henceforth there shall be no more sorrow or suffering. My compassion is now without a specific object, for it was originally intended to save you all. Kingdoms, cities, heads, eyes, wives, children, and hands and feet—I gave these to others countless times. Only now have I finally attained liberation. The Unsurpassed Great..."

“Quiescence—this I shall explain for you. I shall widely open the path of the ambrosia; such great fruits and rewards all arise from giving, precepts, and wisdom, and are born from the six kinds of great patience. They are also attained through great compassion and stainless merit. Having spoken this verse, he remained silent.

At that time, the kings of the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and asuras did not manifest their bodies, yet they rained down celestial flowers as an offering to the Buddha. The trichiliocosm shook in six ways. The Buddha emitted light that illuminated immeasurable lands, so that all those who were ready to be delivered were able to see the Buddha.
○ The seventh turning of the Wheel of Dharma: This is the preaching of the Three Vehicles beneath the Nāgapuṣpa tree, wherein three assemblies deliver sentient beings.
After Maitreya has attained the Way, at that time there shall be a Mara named Mahāsena who governs and transforms by means of the Dharma. Hearing of the Tathāgata...

At that time, [the assembly] heard the sound of his voice and was filled with such joy and exultation that they could not contain themselves. For seven days and seven nights, they neither slept nor rested.
Then, the Māra King, leading countless humans and devas of the desire realm, went to the place where Maitreya Buddha was and paid him respectful homage.
The Honored and Holy Maitreya gradually preached the Dharma to those humans and devas through subtle and wondrous discourses, namely the following treatises:

[He spoke] on the discourse of giving, the discourse of ethical discipline, and the discourse on rebirth in heaven (these explain the dharmas of humans and devas within the desire realm, such as the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths).

[He spoke of] the perception of impurity in sensual desires and the excellence of the essential means of deliverance (these explain the dharmas of the dhyāna heavens, namely the nine perceptions and the eight stages of liberation; the following explains the supramundane dharmas).

At that time, Maitreya, seeing that the people had already resolved their minds, was filled with joy. The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, always preach the Dharma of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, together with the devas.
[The Buddha] extensively analyzed its meaning (this explains the Dharma of the Four Truths for the Śrāvakas of the Hīnayāna).

At that time, eighty-four thousand devaputras on the assembly seat were cleansed of all defilements and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye (the *Sūtra on Attaining Buddhahood* fully explains the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination as well as the factors conducive to Bodhi; that only the Four Truths are mentioned here is because it is an abbreviated account).
At that time, the Great General Māra addressed the people of that realm, saying: "You all must quickly leave the household life.
For this reason: today Maitreya has already crossed to the other shore; he shall likewise lead you across and cause you to reach the other shore."
At that time, in the city of Kukkutavati, there was an elder named Sudhana.
Having heard the command of the Mara King and also having heard the resonance of the Buddha’s voice, he led a multitude of eighty-four thousand beings to the place where Maitreya Buddha was.
He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side. Then Maitreya gradually expounded for him the subtle and wondrous discourse; as for what this discourse was, it was on giving.
[He] preached on the precepts (and so forth).
At that time, Maitreya saw that the minds of the people were opened and their intentions were resolved.

He then extensively analyzed for the sake of the devas and humans the meaning of the Dharma as always taught by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. At that time, eighty thousand [beings] upon the seat...
Four thousand people were cleansed of all defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye.

At that time, Sudhana, together with eighty-four thousand others, came forward and addressed the Buddha, requesting to leave the household life and cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya) thoroughly; they all attained the fruit of Arhatship.
At that time, in Maitreya’s first assembly, eighty-four thousand people attained arhatship.

The practitioner should carefully observe the deluded mind of the present single thought-moment as it follows its respective objects; such is this mind.
Is the mind caused by the mind? Is the mind not caused by the mind? Is the mind both caused by the mind and not caused by the mind?

At that time, the practitioner does not even perceive the mind as saṃsāra, much less perceive the mind as nirvāṇa.

All phenomena, whether karmic offenses or merits, arise from the mind. Apart from the mind, there are no offenses, merits, or any phenomena whatsoever.
If one contemplates that the mind is no-mind, then offenses and merits have no master. Knowing that the nature of offenses and merits is empty, one realizes that all phenomena are empty.
When contemplating in this way, one can destroy all the delusions of birth and death, as well as the false imaginings of the three poisons.
Even the most gravely evil karmas cannot obstruct them. Their body and mind are pure; in every moment of thought, they clearly illuminate all phenomena, neither grasping nor clinging to them.
Through these causes and conditions, they attain correspondence with samādhi.
By the power of samādhi, they immediately behold Samantabhadra and the Buddhas of the ten directions, who stroke their heads and preach the Dharma, such that all dharma-gates manifest before them.
